claude-setup.title: Set up Claude for the first time
claude-setup.subtitle: 15 minutes that improve every future conversation
claude-setup.whatItIs:
15 minutes now save a month of back-and-forth later. Set up your plan, [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]], Memory, Privacy and first Project once — and Claude now knows who you are, what style to answer in, which files to reference. Not a 'generic assistant' — but 'your Claude'.

This tutorial is a mandatory first step for everyone. Without it the other tutorials work 'like for everyone else', not 'like for you'.
claude-setup.approach: Don't skip Privacy settings. Don't write vague Custom Instructions like 'be helpful'. Be specific: your role, your stack, your format preferences. The more concrete, the more Claude adapts.

outcomes.0: Configured Custom Instructions that improve every chat
outcomes.1: Understand Memory — when it helps and when to skip it
outcomes.2: Privacy set according to your preferences
outcomes.3: First Project created with instructions and files
outcomes.4: Know the difference between web, Desktop, and Claude Code

0.question: Open a new chat after setup and ask Claude: 'Who do you think I am based on my instructions?' Check if the answer matches your real role.
0.hint: If Claude's description is vague, your About me needs more specifics.

1.question: Compare: run the same prompt in a fresh chat (no instructions) vs a configured chat. What changed?
1.hint: The difference in quality IS the value of setup.

cs-1.title: Choose your plan
cs-1.why: Before configuring anything, confirm you're on the right plan. Free limits hit fast during active use.

instructions.0: Go to claude.ai → click your avatar (top right) → Settings → Account.
instructions.1: Check your current plan: Free / Pro / Team.
instructions.2: Free: limited daily usage, Sonnet/Haiku models only. Pro ($20/mo): Opus access, higher limits, all features.
instructions.3: Rule: use Free for 1 week. If you hit limits daily → upgrade to Pro.

cs-1.validate: You know your current plan and whether it fits your usage.
cs-1.tip: Don't upgrade immediately. Use Free for a week as a diagnostic — you'll know exactly what limits you actually hit.

cs-2.title: Fill in 'About me' (Custom Instructions)
cs-2.why: This tells Claude who you are. Without it, every answer is generic. With it, every answer is tailored to your role.

instructions.0: Settings → Profile → Custom Instructions → 'About me' field.
instructions.1: Write: your role, industry, main tasks, audience, technical stack.
instructions.2: Keep it under 1500 characters. Dense > long.
instructions.3: Avoid: 'I am a kind person'. Write what changes answers: 'I am a senior iOS developer working on fintech apps.'

cs-2.example:
I'm a [role] at [company type], working on [main product/domain].
My main tasks: [task 1], [task 2], [task 3].
Audience for my output: [who reads your work].
Tech stack: [languages, frameworks, tools].
Working language: [language].
cs-2.validate: The field is saved. Open a new chat and ask: 'What do you know about me?' — Claude should reflect your role.
cs-2.tip: The most useful thing to add is your tech stack. Without it, Claude gives generic recommendations.

cs-3.title: Fill in 'How to respond'
cs-3.why: Controls format, tone, length. The difference between needing to rewrite every answer vs using it directly.

instructions.0: Same Settings → Custom Instructions → 'How to respond' field.
instructions.1: Specify: language, format (bullets/prose), length, tone, and what NOT to do.
instructions.2: Save and test on a real task.

cs-3.example:
Always respond in [language].

Format:
- Lead with the key point, then details.
- Use bullet points for lists.
- Max H3 headings — don't over-structure.

Length: exactly what's needed. If 3 sentences work, don't write 10.

Tone: professional but not dry. No filler phrases like 'Great question!'.

Don't:
- Repeat my question back to me.
- Add disclaimers in obvious cases.
- Use emojis unless I start.
cs-3.validate: New chats follow your format and tone without extra prompting.
cs-3.tip: Every time an answer annoys you — add a rule. Your instructions improve through real use.

cs-4.title: Configure Memory
cs-4.why: Memory lets Claude remember facts across conversations. Useful for recurring context — but not a replacement for Custom Instructions.

instructions.0: Settings → Profile → Memory (if available on your plan).
instructions.1: Enable Memory if you want Claude to remember things you tell it across sessions.
instructions.2: You can view and delete what Claude remembers at any time.
instructions.3: Note: Memory works in claude.ai chats. For Claude Desktop, memory is available via MCP memory server.

cs-4.validate: You know whether Memory is on or off and understand what it stores.
cs-4.tip: Memory is additive — Claude stores things you mention. It won't override your Custom Instructions. Think of it as a sticky notepad.

cs-5.title: Set Privacy settings
cs-5.why: By default, Anthropic may use your conversations to improve models. If you work with sensitive data, opt out.

instructions.0: Settings → Privacy.
instructions.1: Find 'Improve Claude for everyone' or similar training data option.
instructions.2: Toggle OFF if you don't want your conversations used for model training.
instructions.3: Pro and Team plans have stronger privacy defaults than Free.

cs-5.validate: Privacy setting matches your preference. You know what data Anthropic stores.
cs-5.tip: This doesn't affect Claude's quality for you — it only affects whether Anthropic uses your data for future training.

cs-6.title: Create your first Project
cs-6.why: Projects give Claude persistent context, files, and specialized instructions for a specific domain of work. Better than repeating context every chat.

instructions.0: In the left sidebar → click 'New Project'.
instructions.1: Name it by domain: 'Work', 'Coding', 'Writing', etc.
instructions.2: Add Project Instructions: paste a specialized version of your Custom Instructions for this domain.
instructions.3: Upload 1-3 reference files if relevant (style guide, codebase docs, templates).
instructions.4: Open a chat inside the Project — Claude now operates in this specialized context.

cs-6.example:
Project: 'Code Review'
Instructions: You are a senior code reviewer for our React/TypeScript codebase. Focus on: type safety, component reusability, performance. Flag: any direct DOM manipulation, missing error boundaries, unhandled promises. Format: bullet list by severity (Critical / Warning / Info).
cs-6.validate: Project created with instructions. Test: ask 'who are you?' inside the Project — Claude should describe the specialized role.
cs-6.tip: Don't create a project for every task. Start with 1-2 that match your most frequent work contexts.

basics.title: Master the basics of Claude
basics.subtitle: Models, context, system prompt — in practice
basics.whatItIs:
Which Claude model to pick? Opus = your top expert for hard work (strategy, parsing dense PDFs). Sonnet = everyday workhorse (90% of tasks, balance of price and quality). Haiku = lightning-fast for the simple stuff (classification, short answers).

Plus the key concepts: what the [[node:b-context|context window]] is and why AI «forgets» the start of a long conversation, what a [[node:b-system|system prompt]] is and how it changes Claude's behavior. Without this foundation, the other tutorials are just a list of instructions without understanding.
basics.approach: Don't try to memorize theory — go through the steps in Claude and compare answers with your own eyes. Knowledge from practice sticks 10× longer than from an article.

outcomes.0: You consciously choose a model for the task
outcomes.1: You write a structured prompt in 30 seconds
outcomes.2: You know when the context has gone stale and a new chat is needed
outcomes.3: You know the typical scenarios where Claude makes mistakes

0.title: Daily work
0.description: Any work request to Claude now goes through a structured prompt — that's a free +30% quality boost.

1.title: Model selection
1.description: Before a big task — ask yourself: Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku? The right choice saves tokens and time.

2.title: Long conversations
2.description: You notice the model getting confused — open a new chat and bring over only the key conclusions.

pitfalls.0: Studying theory from articles without practice — it won't stick.
pitfalls.1: Using one model for everything — either slow/expensive, or shallow.
pitfalls.2: Dumping 50 files 'just in case' — the model loses focus.

0.question: Take a real work task and write a prompt using the schema 'Role → Task → Format → Constraints'. Send it to Sonnet.
0.hint: If you get a generic answer — check whether you explicitly stated the constraints and format.

1.question: Rewrite your typical one-liner request as a structured prompt. Compare the answers.
1.hint: The contrast should be noticeable — the structured version is usually 2× more detailed.

b-1.title: Sign in to Claude.ai and set up your workspace
b-1.why: This is the entry point — without an account you can't compare models or feel the difference.

instructions.0: Open claude.ai in Chrome or Safari (Firefox works too).
instructions.1: Sign in or register. The Free plan is enough for first steps; Pro is needed for Opus and Projects.
instructions.2: Close the onboarding pop-ups — we'll learn structurally, not through tips.

b-1.validate: You see the 'Reply to Claude…' field and a sidebar with chat history on the left.

troubleshoot.Phone verification requested: This is normal — Anthropic blocks bots. Enter a real number.
troubleshoot.Can't find the model selector: The model button is above the input field or in the top-right corner of the chat.

b-2.title: Compare Haiku, Sonnet and Opus on the same task
b-2.why: Without comparison you won't pick the right model for a task — you'll either overpay or lose depth.

instructions.0: Create 3 chats (one per model: Haiku → Sonnet → Opus).
instructions.1: Send the same prompt below to each — WITHOUT changes.
instructions.2: Compare the answers by: length, specificity, nuance, generation speed.
instructions.3: Note down: which model 'hit' the task best.

b-2.prompt:
Explain why two equally talented junior developers can produce radically different results in the same team.

Give 5 reasons, rank by impact, and for each explain the mechanism. No fluff and no obvious 'communication is important'.
b-2.validate: You have 3 chats with the same prompt and three answers of different depth.
b-2.tip: Haiku is good for drafts and simple tasks, Sonnet is for everyday work, Opus is for complex reasoning and audits.

troubleshoot.Opus not available: Pro/Team only. If on Free — use Sonnet, it's close to Opus for most tasks.

b-3.title: Feel the power of a system prompt
b-3.why: Without a role the model answers like Wikipedia. With a role — like an expert on your task. Quality difference is 30–50%.

instructions.0: Open a new Sonnet chat.
instructions.1: Send the 'naive' prompt (see the block below).
instructions.2: Open a second chat, send the 'prompt with role'.
instructions.3: Compare: how much more concrete the second answer is, tied to constraints, without fluff.

b-3.prompt:
[NAIVE PROMPT — send as-is]
How can I improve my project?

[PROMPT WITH ROLE — send in the second chat]
You are an expert in my domain with a focus on practical results.
Context: describe your task, audience, environment (1–2 sentences).
Task: give 5 recommendations for improving <your object — page / report / process>.
Format: problem → why it hurts the result → what to do.
Constraint: only things that can be implemented in a week without outside help.
b-3.validate: The second answer is specific, tied to constraints, without generic phrases.
b-3.tip: Memorize the structure: context → role → task → format → constraints. That's 80% of a good prompt.

b-4.title: See how the context window works
b-4.why: Understanding the context limit saves you from 'hallucinations' and quality loss on long conversations.

instructions.0: In one chat, ask Claude to briefly introduce itself (see below).
instructions.1: In the same chat, ask 5–7 unrelated questions in a row.
instructions.2: Then ask: 'What was the very first question I asked after your introduction?' — Claude should remember.
instructions.3: This shows that the whole chat is one shared context, not a series of independent requests.

b-4.prompt: Introduce yourself in one line. After that I'll ask several different questions.
b-4.validate: For the last question Claude correctly quotes the first.
b-4.tip: When a chat goes stale (the model gets confused) — open a new one and bring over only the essentials. Don't drag garbage into the context.

b-5.title: Lock it in: pick a model for your real task
b-5.why: Without applying it to your own task, the learning stays theory.

instructions.0: Take YOUR actual task for this week.
instructions.1: Ask yourself: which model is optimal (Haiku / Sonnet / Opus)?
instructions.2: What role and format are needed in the system prompt?
instructions.3: Launch the task right now — while it's fresh.

b-5.validate: You have a running chat with YOUR task and a conscious choice of model + role.
b-5.tip: Continue developing this in 'Prompt Engineering' — we'll go deeper into techniques there.

projects.title: Create your first Project
projects.subtitle: A long-lived workspace with its own context
projects.whatItIs:
You have 5 recurring tasks every week (content, audits, reviews)? Each time you re-explain context to Claude from scratch? A Project turns Claude into a specialist for that specific task — set up once, remembered always.

A Project is a 'folder' in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] with its own instructions and knowledge base files. Every chat inside knows the context without re-briefing.
projects.approach: The key is to choose ONE recurring task for the first Project. Not 'everything about work' — something specific. Narrow focus = high quality.

outcomes.0: Create a Project for a recurring task
outcomes.1: Write Custom Instructions that change answer quality
outcomes.2: Upload the right materials to Project Knowledge
outcomes.3: Know when a Project is needed and when a regular chat is enough

0.title: Regular audits
0.description: A Project with guides and cases — every week you review new material against the same criteria.

1.title: Template documents
1.description: Templates and examples in Knowledge → Claude drafts in your style, you refine.

2.title: Onboarding a new hire
2.description: Share the Project — a new employee immediately gets a 'specialized' Claude for the project.

pitfalls.0: Making one Project for everything. Better 3–5 narrow ones than one universal.
pitfalls.1: Uploading everything into Knowledge — the model loses focus on irrelevant content.
pitfalls.2: Writing instructions like 'be helpful' — that's noise, not a rule.

0.question: Write down your 3 recurring tasks. For the most frequent one — create a Project with minimal instructions and 1–2 files.
0.hint: Recurring = repeats ≥ once a week with a similar process.

1.question: Run your next real task through this Project. Compare with how you did it in a regular chat.
1.hint: If you see no difference — the instructions are weak; refine them based on results.

p-1.title: Confirm Pro/Team plan and open Projects
p-1.why: Projects are only available on paid plans. Without one the next steps are impossible — better to know this upfront.

instructions.0: Go to claude.ai → top-right corner → check your subscription.
instructions.1: If Free — upgrade to Pro ($20/month) or use a team account.
instructions.2: In the left sidebar find 'Projects' → '+ New project'.

p-1.validate: The Project creation form opened with Name and Description fields.

troubleshoot.No Projects section: Are you sure you have Pro? Sometimes you need to log out and back in after an upgrade.

p-2.title: Give the Project a meaningful name and description
p-2.why: The name is an anchor. 'Project 1' you won't remember in 2 weeks; 'Regular Report Audit' you will.

instructions.0: Name: '<what we do> <for whom / what>'. E.g., 'Regular Report Audit' or 'Client Meeting Prep'.
instructions.1: Description: 1–2 lines — what the project is for, who will work in it, what result is expected.
instructions.2: Click Create.

p-2.example:
Name: <Your regular process> for <your domain>
Description: We come here before each iteration to prepare/review results. Core materials and templates are here.
p-2.validate: Project created, you see an empty chat and the 'Project knowledge' / 'Instructions' panel.
p-2.tip: Don't make one Project for everything. Better 3–5 specialized ones than one universal.

p-3.title: Write Custom Instructions
p-3.why: This is the highest-ROI time investment in the Project. Without instructions — a folder with files; with them — a specialized assistant.

instructions.0: Open the Project panel → Custom instructions.
instructions.1: Use the framework below. Fill in your domain.
instructions.2: Save. All future chats in this Project will automatically pick up the instructions.

p-3.prompt:
You are a [role] with [N] years of experience in [niche].

Work context:
- Task type: [the main thing we do]
- Audience for results: [who will read]
- Team style: [how we communicate, format]

Answer format:
- Key point first, then details
- Bullet lists for enumerations
- For recommendations: problem → impact → what to do
- Length: exactly what's needed — no fluff

What you do NOT do:
- Don't give generic advice without grounding in context
- Don't suggest solutions that require resources we don't have
- Don't mix languages unnecessarily
p-3.validate: After saving, send 'who are you?' — Claude should answer as the assigned role, not a generic assistant.
p-3.tip: The most common mistake — overly generic instructions like 'be helpful'. That's noise. Specificity > politeness.

p-4.title: Upload key files to Project knowledge
p-4.why: Files become 'permanent memory' — Claude sees them in all Project chats, no need to repeat context.

instructions.0: In the right Project panel → Project knowledge → Add content / Upload.
instructions.1: Upload 3–7 KEY documents: brand guide, brief, guidelines, reference cases.
instructions.2: Don't upload everything — 5 precise ones beat 50 random ones. Each extra file dilutes focus.
instructions.3: Give each file a clear name — Claude uses it for navigation.

p-4.validate: You see the list of uploaded files in Project knowledge with a 'ready' checkmark.
p-4.tip: For long PDFs — extract the key sections into a separate markdown. Less noise, higher accuracy.

troubleshoot.File too large: Limit is usually 30 MB per file. Compress images or split the PDF.

p-5.title: Run the first real request
p-5.why: Without a real test the Project is just a hypothesis. The request will show how well the instructions and files are tuned.

instructions.0: In the Project open a new chat.
instructions.1: Send the prompt below (adapt it to your task).
instructions.2: Evaluate: did Claude answer in the right format, did it use the uploaded files.

p-5.prompt: Using the materials from knowledge: do your regular task for the input data — [URL / document / description]. Give the result in the format described in the instructions.
p-5.validate: The answer is in the format from the instructions, with explicit references to the uploaded files.
p-5.tip: If Claude doesn't use knowledge — ask explicitly: 'rely on the materials from Project knowledge'.

p-6.title: Iterate the instructions based on results
p-6.why: The first Project is rarely perfect. Real conversations show what needs tightening in the instructions.

instructions.0: After 2–3 chats write down: what does Claude do wrong?
instructions.1: Rephrase each 'wrong' as a rule and add it to Custom instructions.
instructions.2: Save. New chats will immediately apply the changes.

p-6.example:
BEFORE: long fluffy answers
AFTER (added to instructions): 'Never write openers like 'great question'. Get straight to the point.'

BEFORE: generic advice not tied to our stack
AFTER: 'All recommendations — only within the Next.js + Tailwind stack described in knowledge.'
p-6.validate: [[node:instructions|Custom instructions]] grew by 3–5 rules, each born from a real problem.
p-6.tip: A Project is a living document. 10 minutes of instruction review every month saves hours of routine.

p-7.title: Share with the team (if Team plan)
p-7.why: One Project for the team = one quality standard. Everyone stops 'inventing their own Claude'.

instructions.0: Open the Project → Share → Add team members.
instructions.1: Choose access level: Editor (can change instructions) / Viewer (read chats only).
instructions.2: Pin the Project in the team wiki / Notion with a short note: 'when and how to use it'.

p-7.validate: Colleagues see the Project in their lists and can open chats.
p-7.tip: Designate one 'Project curator' — they own the cleanliness of instructions and knowledge. Without a curator the Project degrades within a month.

artifacts.title: Create your first interactive Artifact
artifacts.subtitle: A prototype you can open, click around, and rebuild
artifacts.whatItIs:
You asked Claude for an HTML landing page prototype — it opens in a separate window next to the chat, you can see how it looks and immediately say 'make the button greener'. No copy-pasting to an editor and back. That's an Artifact.

A separate 'canvas' in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] for code, HTML, SVG, documents. Runnable preview right in the browser, iterations with version history, no walls of text in chat.
artifacts.approach: Don't try to 'draw' a perfect final version in the Artifact right away. It's an iteration tool — 3–5 cycles of 'get → poke → rewrite' produce a better result than '10 pages of requirements upfront'.

outcomes.0: You trigger an Artifact intentionally — not by accident
outcomes.1: You build interactive HTML prototypes in minutes
outcomes.2: You use versions for safe iteration
outcomes.3: You share an Artifact with a public link to colleagues

0.title: Idea prototype
0.description: A page / screen concept assembled in 10 minutes in HTML+Tailwind, a live link sent to the team — we discuss the real thing, not a description.

1.title: A shareable document
1.description: A report / guide / meeting summary formatted as an Artifact — it can be opened and read as a standalone document.

2.title: Micro-utility
2.description: A calculator / converter / visualization — assembled in 15 minutes, runs in the browser without a backend.

pitfalls.0: Not specifying the format — Claude will put the code in the chat instead of an Artifact.
pitfalls.1: Asking for 'everything at once' — iterations are more effective.
pitfalls.2: Ignoring versions — you lose good intermediate results.

0.question: Describe to Claude a prototype of one page for your project. Get the Artifact. Revise it 2–3 times.
0.hint: Change ONE thing each time — this shows the power of iteration.

1.question: Rewrite your last Word/Notion documentation as a Markdown Artifact with a table of contents.
1.hint: You'll get a standalone document that's more pleasant to read than in the chat.

a-1.title: Understand when an Artifact is triggered
a-1.why: An Artifact is the 'product' of the work (code / HTML / SVG / Markdown). Not knowing how to trigger it means you keep getting walls of text in the chat.

instructions.0: An artifact is triggered automatically for: code longer than ~20 lines, HTML/React, SVG, Mermaid, long documents.
instructions.1: You can explicitly ask: 'put this in an Artifact'.
instructions.2: The right preview panel opens — it shows the code AND the visual result.

a-1.validate: You understand that an Artifact is a separate panel, not text in the chat.
a-1.tip: If Claude put a large block of code in the chat — ask: 'move this into an Artifact'. It will.

a-2.title: Request the first HTML prototype
a-2.why: A prototype in an Artifact is the fastest way to see an idea 'live' instead of a verbal description.

instructions.0: Open a new chat (can be inside a Project).
instructions.1: Copy the prompt below, substitute your topic.
instructions.2: Wait for generation — a preview opens on the right.
instructions.3: Click 'Preview' / 'Code' — switch between the visual and the code.

a-2.prompt:
Build an interactive single-file HTML prototype as an Artifact.

What we're building: a subscription pricing page with three tiers and a month/year toggle.
Audience: SaaS B2B.
Stack: plain HTML + Tailwind via CDN. No React. No third-party dependencies.

Requirements:
- mobile-first, correct down to 320px
- accessible semantics (label, aria-*)
- 3 states: idle, loading, success
- meaningful copy instead of lorem ipsum

Show the preview immediately.
a-2.validate: You see a preview with three tiers and a toggle; everything works in the preview window.
a-2.tip: If the preview breaks — ask 'fix the preview, I'm getting a blank screen'. Claude will find the bug.

a-3.title: Make a targeted edit
a-3.why: A targeted edit saves tokens and doesn't break the working parts. This is the main way to iterate.

instructions.0: In the chat with the Artifact, ask to change ONE specific thing.
instructions.1: Don't use 'improve everything' — Claude will rewrite half randomly.
instructions.2: Wait for the new version — 'Version 2' will appear at the top of the Artifact.

a-3.prompt: In this Artifact change the primary color to #0F172A. Don't touch the font in the other sections. Make the buttons slightly larger (py-3 → py-4).
a-3.validate: Version 2 contains exactly those three changes; everything else is identical.
a-3.tip: The more precisely you state the edit, the fewer unwanted changes. Compare: 'make it prettier' ❌ vs 'change the radius from 8 to 12, leave everything else' ✅

a-4.title: Use versions for safe experiments
a-4.why: Versioning removes the fear of iteration. Doesn't work — roll back.

instructions.0: Ask Claude to radically rework a section (see prompt).
instructions.1: Get version 3.
instructions.2: At the top of the Artifact click the versions dropdown — switch back to version 2.
instructions.3: Confirm that the previous work is not lost.

a-4.prompt: Now make an experimental alternative: a hero section with a large emotional headline and a video background instead of the gradient. Completely redraw the top of the page.
a-4.validate: You have at least 3 Artifact versions and switching between them works.
a-4.tip: Before experiments, save the version you liked to Notion / GitHub — just in case.

a-5.title: Finalize and take the code
a-5.why: Without moving to a repository, the Artifact stays a demo. This step takes it to real production.

instructions.0: When you're happy with the version — click 'Copy' in the top-right corner of the Artifact.
instructions.1: Paste into your project (a separate file or component).
instructions.2: If the code is React — ask Claude to split it into separate files: 'give me these components as a file structure'.

a-5.validate: Code is pasted into your project and builds without errors.
a-5.tip: Don't copy everything at once. Before copying, ask Claude: 'go through the code and remove unnecessary comments and commented-out junk'.

skills.title: Create your first Skill
skills.subtitle: Turn a routine into a reproducible tool
skills.whatItIs:
Caught yourself writing the same instructions to Claude every time? 'First check X, then do Y, in format Z...'. A Skill is your ready-made checklist for a recurring task: described once, Claude invokes it on its own when the task matches.

A Skill is a folder with SKILL.md and supporting materials. Turns a one-off prompt into a stable tool — consistent quality from run to run, no rewriting rules.
skills.approach: The key is the precise `description` in the frontmatter. Whether the Skill activates depends on it. 'Does an audit' — too vague. 'Use when user asks for audit of X with Y' — a working description.

outcomes.0: You understand when a Skill pays off and when it's overkill
outcomes.1: You write a SKILL.md that Claude activates correctly
outcomes.2: You use supporting files (templates, schemas)
outcomes.3: You define anti-triggers — when the skill should NOT fire

0.title: Regular audits
0.description: A Skill with a fixed report template — every audit comes out in the same format, the team reads consistently.

1.title: Standard task prep
1.description: A 'prep ticket' Skill with a user story + AC + risks template — turns 10 minutes of work into 1 command.

2.title: Reproducible analysis
2.description: A Skill with a baked-in methodology — consistent analysis quality regardless of which team member ran it.

pitfalls.0: Making a Skill for a one-off task — there's no return on investment.
pitfalls.1: A vague description 'does X' — Claude won't understand the trigger.
pitfalls.2: Stuffing everything into SKILL.md — it balloons to an unreadable state.

0.question: Write down your 5 recurring tasks. For the most frequent one, draft a SKILL.md (name, description, 5–7 steps).
0.hint: If the task repeats fewer than 5 times a week — pick a different one.

1.question: Test the Skill: ask Claude a question where it SHOULD activate, and an anti-trigger question where it should NOT.
1.hint: Doesn't activate when it should → loosen the description. Activates when it shouldn't → add anti-triggers.

s-1.title: Choose a routine to formalize
s-1.why: A Skill pays off when the process repeats ≥ 5 times a week. Otherwise you'll spend more time building it than you save.

instructions.0: Write down 3 tasks you repeat regularly with a similar context.
instructions.1: For each, answer: how similar is the process? (≥80% → Skill candidate).
instructions.2: Choose one — the most frequent and stable. Start there.

s-1.example:
Candidates:
1. ✅ Regular audit of your items — every week, same process
2. ❌ 'Help with a task' — too varied, doesn't formalize
3. ✅ Preparing a standard document — several times a day, same template

I choose: preparing the standard document — most frequent.
s-1.validate: One routine is chosen and you can clearly say: 'input → steps → output'.
s-1.tip: A good Skill signal — you're ALREADY catching yourself copying an old prompt.

s-2.title: Launch skill-creator
s-2.why: skill-creator is Anthropic's official skill that asks everything needed and formats SKILL.md correctly.

instructions.0: In claude.ai (Pro+) or Claude Code: ask to activate skill-creator.
instructions.1: If it doesn't activate automatically — write explicitly: 'Use skill anthropic-skills:skill-creator to create a new skill'.
instructions.2: skill-creator will ask a series of questions — answer in detail.

s-2.prompt: Use skill-creator to create a Skill for preparing developer tickets. Ask me all the necessary questions one by one.
s-2.validate: Claude asks questions following the skill-creator structure: name, goal, triggers, steps.

troubleshoot.skill-creator doesn't activate: You may not have access to skills. In Claude Code they're always available; in claude.ai — on paid plans.

s-3.title: Define the role and description
s-3.why: Description = trigger. Whether the Skill fires when needed depends on its precision.

instructions.0: Name: kebab-case, short and clear (e.g., dev-task-prep).
instructions.1: Description: explicit triggers (when to invoke) + explicit anti-triggers (when NOT to invoke).
instructions.2: Use the template below.

s-3.example:
name: dev-task-prep

description: Use this skill when the user asks to convert an idea, bug, or
feature request into a developer-ready ticket. Triggers on phrases like
"prepare a ticket", "make a user story", "turn this into a task for
engineering", or when user pastes raw feature descriptions and wants
structured output.

DO NOT use for: code review, architecture discussions, or when user
explicitly asks for a quick informal note.
s-3.validate: Description contains specific trigger phrases and anti-triggers.
s-3.tip: If your description is a single generic phrase like 'helps with tasks' — the Skill will fire on everything. Be specific.

s-4.title: Describe the step-by-step workflow
s-4.why: Workflow is a 'recipe'. The clearer it is, the more stable the result from run to run.

instructions.0: Describe 5–8 steps Claude should execute.
instructions.1: For each step: what it does + what output it passes to the next step.
instructions.2: The final step — format of the output.

s-4.example:
## Workflow

1. **Clarify the idea**: if description is shorter than 2 lines — ask 3 clarifying questions (context, user goal, constraints).
2. **Formulate User Story**: format 'As a [role] I want [action] so that [value]'.
3. **Acceptance Criteria**: 4–7 points in Given/When/Then format.
4. **Technical notes**: what we touch / what we do NOT touch (if applicable).
5. **Edge cases**: 3–5 negative scenarios.
6. **Estimate**: XS/S/M/L/XL with a one-line justification.
7. **DoD**: 3–5 'done when…' points.

## Output format
Markdown, ready to paste into Linear/Jira.
s-4.validate: The workflow reads like a recipe: the cook (Claude) knows each step.
s-4.tip: If there are > 10 steps — the Skill is too big. Split into two linked Skills.

s-5.title: Add templates/ — templates for repeatability
s-5.why: Templates move details out of SKILL.md and keep it short. They also guarantee a consistent format.

instructions.0: Create a file templates/ticket.md inside the skill folder.
instructions.1: Describe in it exactly the format that should appear in the output.
instructions.2: In SKILL.md refer to the template: 'follow the format from templates/ticket.md'.

s-5.example:
# templates/ticket.md

## User Story
As a {role}, I want {action} so that {value}.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Given {context}, When {action}, Then {outcome}
- [ ] ...

## Technical notes
**Touch:** ...
**Don't touch:** ...

## Edge cases
- ...

## Estimate: {XS|S|M|L|XL}
{Reason in one line}

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Tests pass
- [ ] Code reviewed
- [ ] ...
s-5.validate: The template is saved and SKILL.md references it.
s-5.tip: A template is a contract. It's easier to change than to rewrite SKILL.md every time.

s-6.title: Test the trigger
s-6.why: A Skill that doesn't activate when needed is dead. Trigger testing is mandatory.

instructions.0: Write Claude a natural phrase that the Skill should fire on.
instructions.1: Check: did it activate or not.
instructions.2: Then — a phrase it should NOT fire on (anti-trigger). Confirm Claude doesn't activate the Skill.
instructions.3: If triggers misbehave — go back to step 3 and tighten the description.

s-6.example:
✅ Should fire: 'Help me turn this idea into a ticket for developers'
✅ Should fire: 'Make a user story with AC from this feature description'
❌ Should NOT: 'Tell me in general terms how to write user stories' (that's a learning request, not ticket prep)
s-6.validate: The Skill fires on all ✅ and does not fire on ❌.
s-6.tip: The most common problem — the Skill fires too often. The fix is to add more anti-triggers to the description.

s-7.title: Run it on a real task and improve
s-7.why: A real test surfaces things invisible in synthetic examples.

instructions.0: Take a real task from your backlog.
instructions.1: Run it through the Skill 2–3 times.
instructions.2: Where the result is weak — add a rule to the Workflow or an anti-trigger to the description.
instructions.3: After 5–10 runs the Skill stabilizes.

s-7.validate: The Skill is used in real work; you're not writing the same prompt by hand.
s-7.tip: Share the Skill with the team via the repository (skills/). One Skill × 5 people = 5× the return.

skills.trigger: You notice you write the same checklist «first X, then Y, in format Z» every time.
inputs: A reference example «what good looks like»
outputs: Ready SKILL.md with metadata + assets
Skill that Claude triggers itself on matching tasks
Versioning for the team
skills.savings: ~10-15 min per recurring task + a single quality bar

claude-code.title: Install and configure Claude Code
claude-code.subtitle: A full AI agent in the terminal
claude-code.whatItIs:
You know VS Code Copilot that completes lines of code? [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] does the same, but 10× the scope: reads your whole project, edits dozens of files, runs commands, does refactors. And it lives in your terminal, not your editor.

Anthropic's CLI tool for working with Claude directly in the terminal. Uses [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]], sub-agents, [[node:mcp|MCP servers]] and [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] as project memory. Turns the terminal into a full AI-powered development environment.
claude-code.approach: Don't try to master everything at once. Install → run [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] → try one real edit → tune [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]]. Most of Claude Code's power unlocks through the CLAUDE.md you write for your own project.

outcomes.0: Installed Claude Code and launched it in your project
outcomes.1: Generated CLAUDE.md with /init and tuned it
outcomes.2: Configured basic permissions for safe commands
outcomes.3: Understand the main slash commands and modes (Plan / Fast)

0.title: Code review
0.description: claude in the repo → /review → a structured audit at the level of an experienced developer in minutes.

1.title: Safe refactoring
1.description: Plan mode → a change plan → you approve → execution. No surprises in the code.

2.title: Auto-documentation
2.description: Add Hooks: README and CHANGELOG update automatically whenever files change.

pitfalls.0: Running outside a git repo — you lose history context.
pitfalls.1: Without CLAUDE.md the model rediscovers the project every time.
pitfalls.2: Overly broad permissions (allow: [Bash(*)]) — loss of control.

0.question: In your real repo: run claude → /init → tune CLAUDE.md (add a 'forbidden' section with your rules).
0.hint: At least 3 lines in the forbidden section — this shows the result immediately.

1.question: Make a small edit (rename a variable) through Plan mode. Compare with doing the same in normal mode.
1.hint: Plan mode = 'show the plan first, I'll approve'. Very quickly becomes the default.

cc-1.title: Install Node.js (if not present)
cc-1.why: Claude Code is an npm package. Without Node.js it won't run.

instructions.0: Check: open terminal → `node -v`.
instructions.1: If there's no version or it's < 18 — install a fresh Node.js.
instructions.2: macOS: `brew install node`. Windows: download the installer from nodejs.org.

cc-1.validate: In the terminal `node -v` shows 18.x or higher.

troubleshoot.command not found: node: Restart the terminal after installing. Or check PATH.

cc-2.title: Install Claude Code globally
cc-2.why: A global install lets you call `claude` from any folder.

instructions.0: In the terminal: `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`.
instructions.1: Wait ~30 seconds.
instructions.2: Verify: `claude --version`.

cc-2.validate: `claude --version` prints the version number without errors.

troubleshoot.EACCES permission denied: macOS/Linux: use `sudo npm install -g ...` or configure npm prefix to your own ~/.npm-global.
troubleshoot.EEXIST file already exists: An old version is sitting there. Remove: `npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, then install again.

cc-3.title: Launch in a repository and authenticate
cc-3.why: Claude Code works in the context of a folder. Authentication is once per machine.

instructions.0: Navigate to any project folder: `cd ~/projects/my-project`.
instructions.1: Run: `claude`.
instructions.2: On first run a browser opens for Anthropic authentication — sign in.
instructions.3: After that you're in an interactive Claude session.

cc-3.validate: The terminal shows a Claude prompt; you can type messages.
cc-3.tip: Works best in a git repository — Claude sees the history and diff. Outside a repo it loses half its features.

cc-4.title: Generate CLAUDE.md with /init
cc-4.why: CLAUDE.md is the project's 'personality'. Claude reads it on every launch and doesn't ask about the obvious.

instructions.0: In the Claude session type: `/init`.
instructions.1: Claude scans the project and proposes a CLAUDE.md draft.
instructions.2: Read it. Remove what's inaccurate, add rules and forbidden actions (see example).
instructions.3: Save. The file lives in the project root.

cc-4.example:
# CLAUDE.md

## Stack
- Next.js 14, App Router
- Tailwind CSS
- TypeScript (strict)

## Conventions
- NEVER use `any`. Only `unknown` or strict types.
- Tests — Vitest, not Jest. Files next to source: `foo.ts` + `foo.test.ts`.
- All components — functional with TypeScript.

## Forbidden
- Don't add extra UI libraries. Tailwind + our components only.
- Don't rewrite `auth/` without sign-off — there's legal compliance there.

## Entry points
- src/app/(routes)/page.tsx — main
- src/lib/api.ts — all external calls (no direct fetch outside)
cc-4.validate: CLAUDE.md is in the repo root, filled with rules specific to YOUR project.
cc-4.tip: Don't describe the obvious. 'This is a React project' — noise. 'Only functional components' — a rule.

cc-5.title: Run /security-review on a branch
cc-5.why: A useful built-in workflow — lets you feel the power of slash commands.

instructions.0: Make a simple code change, commit it (but don't push).
instructions.1: In the Claude session: `/security-review`.
instructions.2: Claude analyzes the diff and produces a list of security findings.
instructions.3: Study the report — even if the code is clean you'll see what Claude can do.

cc-5.tip: Build /security-review into a pre-merge habit for serious changes. More thorough than any junior.

cc-6.title: Configure your first Hook
cc-6.why: Hooks automate behavior you don't want to rely on Claude 'remembering'.

instructions.0: Create the file `.claude/settings.json` (or open the existing one).
instructions.1: Add a PostToolUse:Write hook — it will run prettier after every file edit.
instructions.2: Restart claude.
instructions.3: Make a test edit — you'll see prettier ran automatically.

cc-6.validate: After every file edit, Claude automatically runs prettier.
cc-6.tip: Hooks = 'junior's discipline'. Linter, tests, typecheck — all in hooks. The model won't forget.

troubleshoot.Hook doesn't fire: Check — is settings.json valid JSON? Restart `claude`.
troubleshoot.Hook complains about the path: Use `$CLAUDE_FILE_PATH` (available env variable), don't guess the path.

cc-7.title: Create a custom subagent
cc-7.why: A subagent takes over a large task and doesn't pollute the main context. The best investment in productivity.

instructions.0: Create the file `.claude/agents/code-reviewer.md`.
instructions.1: Describe the role, tools, and instructions (see example below).
instructions.2: In the chat ask: 'run code-reviewer on the current changes'.
instructions.3: Claude will invoke the subagent, which returns a structured report.

cc-7.example:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Use when user asks to review code changes, current diff, or specific files. Output is a structured list of issues by severity.
tools: Read, Bash
---

You are a senior code reviewer. Your job:

1. Read the diff with `git diff`.
2. For each change, check: correctness, security, readability, tests.
3. Return a markdown report:
   - 🔴 Critical (blocks merge)
   - 🟡 Important (should fix)
   - 🟢 Nit (optional)
4. For each issue: file:line + what's wrong + how to fix.

Do NOT make architectural arguments — focus on the diff in front of you.
Do NOT rewrite code yourself — only point out issues.
cc-7.validate: The subagent activates and produces a structured report.
cc-7.tip: The description is again critical. The parent agent uses it to decide whether to delegate.

cc-8.title: Lock it in — embed Claude Code in your workflow
cc-8.why: Without building it into a habit, Claude Code stays a toy. The goal — it's part of your workday.

instructions.0: Set up 3 regular scenarios: e.g., '/security-review before PR', 'code-reviewer on big diffs', '/init on new projects'.
instructions.1: Document them in the team README.
instructions.2: After a week — calculate how much time you saved.

cc-8.validate: You have 3 scenarios you use by habit, without consciously thinking 'let me try Claude'.
cc-8.tip: Next step — MCP. Connecting Linear/Figma/DB turns Claude Code from a code assistant into a product assistant.

mcp.title: Connect your first MCP server
mcp.subtitle: Give Claude access to external systems
mcp.whatItIs:
You know how USB-C is one cable for everything — laptop, monitor, headphones, charger? MCP is 'USB-C for AI'. One standard so Claude can connect to anything: your Linear, Notion, database, files, GitHub — without copy-paste or homemade integrations.

[[node:mcp|MCP (Model Context Protocol)]] is Anthropic's open standard. Through an MCP server, Claude sees your real tools and works directly inside them.
mcp.approach: Start with an existing server (filesystem or github), not your own. First understand the ecosystem and data formats through a working example, then design your own.

outcomes.0: Understand MCP architecture: server / client / transport
outcomes.1: Connected an existing MCP server to Claude Code
outcomes.2: Tell the difference between stdio and HTTP/SSE transports
outcomes.3: Can debug 'why MCP doesn't see data'

0.title: Context from a tracker
0.description: MCP to a task tracker → Claude sees fresh tickets, can comment and suggest decompositions.

1.title: Documentation in context
1.description: MCP to Confluence/Notion → Claude answers with your internal documentation in mind.

2.title: Code access
2.description: MCP to GitHub → Claude sees PRs, can comment, make review observations.

pitfalls.0: Connecting everything — each server loads on startup.
pitfalls.1: Destructive tools without a confirm step — risky.
pitfalls.2: Storing tokens in the project settings.json (will end up in git) instead of settings.local.json.

0.question: Set up an MCP server for filesystem. Ask Claude to find all .md files in your documents folder and make a table of contents.
0.hint: Filesystem is the safest for a first MCP. Completely local.

1.question: Connect MCP to one external system you use (github / linear / notion). Ask a real question: 'what's happening in project X'.
1.hint: If nothing found — check /mcp in Claude Code: did the server start? Are tools visible?

m-1.title: Understand why you need MCP
m-1.why: Without MCP, Claude only sees what you paste manually. With MCP — it lives in your environment.

instructions.0: Write down 3 tools you use daily (Linear, Figma, DB, Slack...).
instructions.1: For each: 'what could Claude do if it could see this?'.
instructions.2: Choose ONE — the most frequent. Start there.

m-1.example:
Candidates:
1. ✅ Linear — daily, lots of context in tickets
2. ✅ Figma — weekly, designs, need handoff to code
3. ❌ Notion — rarely

I'll start with: Linear.
m-1.tip: Good sign: you catch yourself copy-pasting from this tool into a Claude chat. That's the MCP ROI signal.

m-2.title: Find an existing server in the catalog
m-2.why: 95% of services already have a server. Don't write your own — it's a waste of time.

instructions.0: Open the Anthropic MCP catalog or the official docs of your chosen service.
instructions.1: Find the server for your tool.
instructions.2: Copy the connection configuration.

m-2.validate: You have a snippet for settings/config with the url, tokens, and scope.

troubleshoot.No server in the catalog: Search community repos or MCP-registry. As a last resort — write your own, but that's advanced.

m-3.title: Create an access token / API key
m-3.why: The token is the security checkpoint. What MCP can read and change depends on its scope.

instructions.0: In the service (Linear/Figma/etc.) → Settings → API → Create token.
instructions.1: Grant the minimum necessary permissions. Prefer read-only; if writes are needed — a separate token.
instructions.2: Copy the token somewhere safe (1Password / Bitwarden). It's shown ONCE.

m-3.validate: Token created, stored in the password manager, permissions are the minimum needed.
m-3.tip: For the first connection — read-only. You can add write permission later, once you trust the server.

troubleshoot.Not sure which scopes I need: Take 'read-only on main resources' (e.g., Issues for Linear). Expand later.

m-4.title: Connect the MCP server to Claude Code or claude.ai
m-4.why: Configuration is the most common source of errors. Follow the checklist.

instructions.0: Open `~/.config/claude-code/mcp.json` (Code) or Settings → Connectors (claude.ai).
instructions.1: Add the server configuration block (see example).
instructions.2: Insert the token from your password manager (DON'T hardcode it — use ENV).
instructions.3: Restart Claude.

m-4.validate: Claude restarted without errors; logs contain a line like `connected: linear` or similar.

troubleshoot.Server doesn't start: Check JSON validity and that the token is set in ENV. Run `npx <package>` separately — you'll see the error.
troubleshoot.Authentication failed: Token was copied with a space or has the wrong scope. Create a new one and verify.

m-5.title: Check the available tools
m-5.why: Without checking you don't know what the MCP server actually offers. This is the first thing to do.

instructions.0: In the chat ask: 'show me what tools are available via MCP'.
instructions.1: Claude will list tools with their parameter schemas.
instructions.2: Read — mark 2–3 that you definitely need.

m-5.prompt: Show the list of MCP tools available to you. For each — name and short description from the schema.
m-5.validate: You received a list of tools with descriptions.
m-5.tip: If there are too many tools — ask 'keep only those for Issues and Comments active'. Less noise.

m-6.title: Make the first real request with MCP
m-6.why: A real request shows the actual value. Without it, MCP is setup for the sake of setup.

instructions.0: Take a typical task from your practice (see examples).
instructions.1: Send Claude the request — it will choose the right MCP tools automatically.
instructions.2: Evaluate: does the answer rely on fresh data from the service, not guesses.

m-6.example:
Linear: 'Show all P0 bugs in the current sprint, grouped by component, with a short risk assessment for each.'

Figma: 'Open node [URL] and convert it to a React component in our design system style.'

GitHub: 'Give me a summary of all PRs opened in the last 7 days, with authors and CI status.'
m-6.validate: The answer contains fresh, accurate data from the service.
m-6.tip: If Claude is uncertain — ask 'verify through MCP, not from memory'. Sometimes the model gets lazy and guesses.

m-7.title: Security audit of the connection
m-7.why: The MCP server sees what the token sees. Checking scope = insurance.

instructions.0: Open the token panel in the service → check what permissions it has.
instructions.1: If there's write permission — ask yourself: do I actually need write?
instructions.2: If in doubt — recreate the token with fewer permissions.
instructions.3: Enable 2FA in the service if not already.

m-7.validate: The token has exactly the scopes you use, no more.
m-7.tip: Never use one token for different servers. One service = one token. This simplifies revocation.

mcp.trigger: You want Claude to see your Linear / Notion / DB directly — no more copy-paste briefings.

instructions.title: Configure Custom Instructions
instructions.subtitle: Make Claude 'yours' at the profile level
instructions.whatItIs:
Tired of explaining to Claude every time «I'm in marketing, answer briefly in English, no fluff»? [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]] is the field in your [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] profile where it's written once. Applies to ALL chats automatically.

Two fields: 'About me' (who you are) and 'How to respond' (how to answer). Fill them once — every Claude response now factors in your role, style, and constraints. Base investment: 5 minutes now, payoff forever.
instructions.approach: Fill them concisely, not at length — length doesn't equal quality. The most useful things: your role/industry/stack + 3–5 rules like 'don't give disclaimers in obvious cases'. Every time an answer annoys you — add a rule.

outcomes.0: Know the difference between global and Project instructions
outcomes.1: Filled in 'About me' so that answers actually change
outcomes.2: Described the format and tone in 'How to respond'
outcomes.3: Can iterate instructions based on real conversation results

0.title: Quality from the first message
0.description: Without instructions every chat starts with a briefing. With them — Claude is already 'specialized' for you.

1.title: Consistent format across the team
1.description: Share a common instruction template — the whole team gets Claude answering in the same style.

2.title: Less editing
2.description: The right instructions make the first draft usable without further edits.

pitfalls.0: Writing 'be helpful / friendly' — that's noise, not a rule.
pitfalls.1: Long essays instead of bullet points — the model loses focus.
pitfalls.2: Not iterating — the first version is rarely perfect.

0.question: Fill in the global Custom Instructions using the template: role, experience, audience, recurring tasks, stack, language.
0.hint: Don't write 'I'm a good person'. Write what changes the answers.

1.question: Run a typical task before and after Custom Instructions. Compare 3 answers: what improved.
1.hint: If nothing changed — the instructions are weak; add specifics.

i-1.title: Open profile settings
i-1.why: Custom Instructions at the profile level apply to ALL chats — this is the baseline investment.

instructions.0: In claude.ai → click the avatar (top right) → Settings.
instructions.1: Find the 'Profile' / 'Custom Instructions' section.
instructions.2: You see two fields: 'About me' and 'How to respond'.

i-1.validate: You see a form with two text fields.

troubleshoot.Can't see Settings: Sometimes the section is called Preferences. Or it's hidden behind '···'. Look carefully.

i-2.title: Fill in 'About me'
i-2.why: This is context about you. Without it Claude answers 'for everyone'; with it — for exactly your role.

instructions.0: Describe: role, experience, domain, main tasks, audience for your work.
instructions.1: Don't write 'I'm a good person'. Write what changes Claude's answers.
instructions.2: Length — up to 1500 characters. Density > length.

i-2.example:
<Describe your role in one line: title + industry + context.>
<Your experience: years, key strengths.>
Audience for my output: <who you exchange results with>.

I regularly work with:
- <your regular task #1>
- <your regular task #2>
- <your regular task #3>

<If relevant — your tech stack / tools / systems.>
Working language: <language / languages you work in>.
i-2.validate: 'About me' is filled in, describing things that change the answers (role, domain, stack, work format).
i-2.tip: The most useful thing to add is a specific stack/tools. Without them, Claude recommends generically.

i-3.title: Fill in 'How to respond'
i-3.why: This field controls style and format. It determines how much you can use answers without editing.

instructions.0: Describe: language, length, format, tone, what NOT to do.
instructions.1: Use the template below — it covers 90% of cases.
instructions.2: Save and test on a typical task.

i-3.example:
Always respond in [language]. Technical terms — don't translate if the translation is awkward.

Format:
- Key point first, then details.
- Bullet lists for enumerations.
- H3 headings max, don't over-structure.

Length: exactly what's needed. If you can say it in 3 sentences — don't write 10.

Tone: professional, not stiff. But not dry either — some irony is fine where appropriate.

Do NOT:
- Write openers like 'Great question!'
- Repeat my request back to me.
- Use emojis in body text (unless I start).
- Give 'consult an expert' disclaimers in obvious cases.
i-3.validate: The field is saved; new chats follow your format and tone.
i-3.tip: If something still annoys you in the answers — that's a signal to add a new rule.

i-4.title: Test run on 3 different tasks
i-4.why: Without testing, instructions may 'not kick in'. The test is your mirror.

instructions.0: Open 3 new chats and set 3 different tasks (everyday, professional, creative).
instructions.1: Check: does each answer match the instructions.
instructions.2: Where it doesn't — write down and refine the instructions.

i-4.example:
Test 1: a technical task — example from your domain
Test 2: a professional task — example from your domain
Test 3: a creative task — example from your domain
i-4.validate: All three answers are in the right language, format, tone.
i-4.tip: A checklist of rules born from real problems = the best kind of instructions. Don't write 'be friendly' — write 'don't use the word disclaimer'.

i-5.title: Adapt at the Project level (if you have one)

instructions.0: Open your Project → Custom Instructions.
instructions.1: Here add only what is specific to the Project's NICHE.
instructions.2: Global rules (language, format) are already inherited — don't duplicate.

i-5.example:
[In Project '<your regular task>']

In addition to my global instructions:

In this Project you are a specialist in my domain with a specific focus (describe).

Format of each result:
1. Context / input data
2. Problem or principle that was violated
3. Impact (high / medium / low)
4. Recommendation (concrete action, not an abstraction)

Draw on the materials from Project knowledge.
i-5.validate: The Project works in a specialized mode; global rules are not broken.
i-5.tip: Test: ask in the Project 'who are you?'. It should answer as the specialized role, not a generic assistant.

prompting.title: Level up your prompt engineering
prompting.subtitle: Turn 'I asked' into 'I got predictable quality'
prompting.whatItIs:
Same request to Claude — one gives a hollow 'here's a general overview of the topic...', another gives a concrete plan with numbers. The only difference is the wording. That's prompt engineering — the skill of 'how to ask so AI answers usefully'.

Five levers: structure, context, examples, role, constraints. Same AI, results 5-10× apart — all the difference is in how you phrase the request.
prompting.approach: Don't study techniques from a list. Take your REAL weak prompt and upgrade it step by step. Each step = +one technique. By the end of the tutorial this prompt works 3–5× better — and you understand why.

outcomes.0: You write prompts using the schema context → role → task → format → constraints
outcomes.1: You use XML tags to separate instructions from data
outcomes.2: You apply few-shot when the model doesn't catch the pattern
outcomes.3: You enable Chain of Thought on analytical tasks

0.title: Any non-trivial task
0.description: Before a complex request — 30 seconds on structure. The cheapest way to raise quality.

1.title: Analytical tasks
1.description: Comparisons, assessments, conclusions — always with Chain of Thought or Tree of Thought.

2.title: Reproducible formats
2.description: If the result needs to be in JSON/table — describe the schema explicitly and give 1–2 examples.

pitfalls.0: A one-liner 'do it well' — the most common source of bad answers.
pitfalls.1: Too many few-shot examples — the model 'confuses' patterns.
pitfalls.2: CoT on simple tasks — just extra noise.

0.question: Find your weak prompt from history. Rewrite it using the full schema (role/context/task/format/constraints). Compare answers.
0.hint: The worse the original prompt — the more noticeable the upgrade effect.

1.question: Take a complex analytical task. Do it TWICE: without CoT and with a CoT trigger. Measure the difference.
1.hint: CoT trigger: 'Think step by step before answering' at the end of the prompt.

pr-1.title: Take your real prompt
pr-1.why: Learning on your own tasks is 10× more effective than on synthetic ones. Find yours.

instructions.0: Find in the chat history a prompt that Claude answered 'not great'.
instructions.1: Copy it into notes — we'll upgrade it step by step.
instructions.2: Write down what in the answer you did NOT like (vague? generic? wrong format?).

pr-1.example:
My prompt: 'Help me improve my project'.
What I didn't like: the answer — generic textbook advice. Not tied to my product, audience, or tools.
pr-1.validate: You have a real 'weak' prompt in hand and a list of complaints about the answer.
pr-1.tip: The worse the prompt — the more noticeable the upgrade. Don't pick a good one — pick a typical one.

pr-2.title: Apply the basic structure
pr-2.why: The structure 'context → role → task → format → constraints' solves 80% of weak-prompt problems.

instructions.0: Rewrite your prompt using the template below.
instructions.1: Fill in all fields — missing ones = weak spots.
instructions.2: Send to Claude and compare with the previous answer.

pr-2.example:
[CONTEXT]
<Briefly describe your project, audience, current stage (1–2 sentences).>

[ROLE]
You are an expert in my domain with a specific focus (describe).

[TASK]
Give 5 recommendations for <your object>. Input data: [URL / document / description].

[FORMAT]
For each problem:
- what's wrong (1 line)
- impact (high / medium / low)
- what to do (concrete action, not abstraction)

[CONSTRAINTS]
- Only things that can be implemented within <realistic timeframe>
- No recommendations requiring a fundamental rewrite
- Draw on proven principles / standards in your domain
pr-2.validate: The answer is specific, tied to context, in the right format.
pr-2.tip: If even one field is empty — fill it in. Each field improves answer accuracy.

pr-3.title: Add XML tags for long prompts
pr-3.why: XML markup separates instructions from data. Claude is trained on it — understands it perfectly.

instructions.0: If the prompt contains data / examples / code — wrap them in XML tags.
instructions.1: Use meaningful tag names: <context>, <task>, <example>, <code>.
instructions.2: This is especially important when instructions and data could get mixed up.

pr-3.example:
<context>
<Brief description of the task and domain.>
</context>

<input_data>
[all the material here — text, description, code or other inputs]
</input_data>

<task>
Find the critical problems in this material.
</task>

<format>
- problem
- impact
- recommendation
</format>
pr-3.validate: The prompt reads clearly: where are the instructions, where is the data.
pr-3.tip: XML is for long prompts with data. For short ones — overkill.

pr-4.title: Give a few-shot example
pr-4.why: 'Input → output' examples are stronger than any description. This is the most underrated technique.

instructions.0: Give 1–3 examples: what input → what output.
instructions.1: Examples — for the SAME type of task as the real request.
instructions.2: After the examples — your real request.

pr-4.example:
<example>
Input: "SaaS login form"
Output:
- Problem: 6 fields including password repeat and captcha — that causes 30% drop-off at this step.
- Impact: high — this is a critical funnel point.
- Recommendation: remove captcha (show only on suspicion), remove 'repeat password' (there's a 'show password' option).
</example>

<example>
Input: "SaaS landing hero section"
Output:
- Problem: headline 'Business Solution' — generic, doesn't explain the value.
- Impact: high — the user doesn't understand what the product is.
- Recommendation: rewrite in the format '<verb> <result> <in time>' — e.g., 'Track your team's work hours in 5 minutes a day'.
</example>

Now do the same for my material: [URL / document / description]
pr-4.validate: The answer is in exactly the same format as the examples. The style is copied.
pr-4.tip: 2 examples are stronger than 5. Too many examples — the model 'confuses' patterns.

pr-5.title: Add Chain of Thought (for analytical tasks)
pr-5.why: CoT improves accuracy on complex tasks by 1.2–1.4×. For simple ones — just extra noise.

instructions.0: If the task requires REASONING (not 'extract a fact'), add a CoT trigger.
instructions.1: Simple trigger: 'Think step by step before answering'.
instructions.2: Advanced: give explicit reasoning steps.

pr-5.example:
Task: evaluate which of three architectures is faster for our use case.

Think step by step before answering:
1. Write out my load parameters (RPS, request size, write frequency).
2. For each architecture — where is the bottleneck under this load.
3. Which architecture is easier to scale vertically / horizontally.
4. Only then — the recommendation and justification.
pr-5.validate: The answer shows the reasoning process, then the final recommendation.
pr-5.tip: Don't use CoT for creative or short tasks — it'll be a 'parody of reasoning'.

pr-6.title: Compare 'before' and 'after'
pr-6.why: Without an explicit comparison you won't feel the effect — and won't lock in the skill.

instructions.0: Run the original 'weak' prompt in a new chat.
instructions.1: Run the improved one in another.
instructions.2: Put them side by side. Note: length doesn't matter, accuracy and usability do.
instructions.3: Save the improved version as a template.

pr-6.validate: A clear qualitative difference is visible. The improved version is usable without editing; the original — isn't.
pr-6.tip: Copy prompt templates into Notion / your 'prompt-library' repository. In a year that's your main asset.

pr-7.title: Turn it into a ready-to-use template
pr-7.why: One tuned prompt = a template you'll use hundreds of times. Don't lose it.

instructions.0: Replace specific values with placeholders [...] (product, link, audience).
instructions.1: Save in your library (Notion, text file, snippets).
instructions.2: Use it every time — don't write from scratch.

pr-7.validate: The template is in your library; you can apply it in 30 seconds.
pr-7.tip: Next — the 'Ready prompts' section in the map: 10 templates for typical tasks.

agents.title: Create your first agent
agents.subtitle: Turn a routine into a delegatable function
agents.whatItIs: A sub-agent in [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] is an isolated 'specialist' that the main Claude delegates to for a specific type of task. The agent has its own role, tools, and checklists. It turns a repeating process into a single command.
agents.approach: Don't create an agent 'for the future'. Create it for a specific routine you're doing manually 5+ times a week right now. The description is the most important thing: whether the agent activates depends on it. If it's generic ('does X') — it will never fire.

outcomes.0: Understand when an agent is needed and when a Skill is enough
outcomes.1: Wrote an agent spec: name / description / system prompt / workflow
outcomes.2: Described anti-patterns — where an agent does NOT help
outcomes.3: Launched the agent on a real task and measured the effect

0.title: Code review
0.description: Sub-agent with a review checklist → run before merge, get a filtered report.

1.title: Audit agent
1.description: Regular audit against fixed criteria → one trigger instead of a long prompt.

2.title: Researcher
2.description: Agent for gathering and synthesizing sources with web search → a report with links instead of manual work.

pitfalls.0: Making an agent for a task that comes up once a month — no ROI.
pitfalls.1: Vague description — the agent will never activate.
pitfalls.2: Trusting the agent alone — it doesn't replace the architectural thinking of an expert.

0.question: Choose one real routine (≥ 3 times a week). Write an agent spec: name, description (with specific triggers), system prompt, 5–7 workflow steps.
0.hint: The description should be such that reading it, you'd know exactly when to invoke it.

1.question: Run the agent on 3 different inputs. Check — it activates ONLY when it should. If not — tighten the description / add anti-triggers.
1.hint: Anti-triggers (what should NOT trigger it) matter more than positive triggers.

ag-1.title: Find a suitable routine
ag-1.why: A good agent automates a repeating process. Without a routine — no agent.

instructions.0: Write down processes you repeat 3+ times a week with a similar context.
instructions.1: For each: inputs, steps, outputs should be stable 80% of the time.
instructions.2: Choose ONE — the most frequent and stable.

ag-1.example:
Candidates:
1. ✅ Code review for PRs — daily, same steps
2. ✅ Regular audit of your materials — weekly, same steps
3. ❌ 'Help me discuss an idea' — too varied, not an agent

I choose: code-reviewer.
ag-1.validate: A specific routine is chosen with a clear 'input → steps → output'.
ag-1.tip: If the task requires creativity and context — that's your job, not the agent's. Agents are about repeatability.

ag-2.title: Describe the role and goal
ag-2.why: Without a clear role the agent will 'try to do everything'. Trying to do everything — it does everything poorly.

instructions.0: Write down: who is this agent (role), who does it serve (consumer), what does it output.
instructions.1: Limit the scope explicitly: what the agent does NOT do.
instructions.2: Use the template below.

ag-2.example:
Name: code-reviewer
Role: Senior code reviewer, focused on security and readability.
Consumer: Me — a developer, before opening a PR.
Output: Markdown report with a list of issues by severity (🔴/🟡/🟢).

NOT scope:
- Does not write code (only flags problems)
- Does not do architectural review (only the diff)
- Does not optimize performance (unless there are clear regressions)
ag-2.validate: Name + role + consumer + output + explicit NOT-scope written down.
ag-2.tip: NOT-scope protects against scope creep. Without it, the agent 'does everything' within a month — and does it poorly.

ag-3.title: Write the description (trigger)
ag-3.why: The description is the agent's most important artifact. Whether the parent agent delegates to it depends on this.

instructions.0: Describe: WHEN the agent should activate (trigger phrases / contexts).
instructions.1: Describe: WHEN it should NOT fire (anti-triggers).
instructions.2: Give 2–3 examples of explicit 'call me' / 'don't call me'.

ag-3.example:
description: Use when user asks to review code changes, current diff, a
specific PR, or files in their working tree. Triggers on phrases like
"review my changes", "check this PR", "code review", "look at the diff".

DO NOT use for: writing new code, architecture discussions, debugging
help, or when user explicitly asks for "quick check" — they want a
human glance, not a structured review.
ag-3.validate: Description contains specific triggers and explicit anti-triggers with examples.
ag-3.tip: The description is the most common failure point of an agent. Test it on 5+ real requests.

ag-4.title: Describe the step-by-step workflow
ag-4.why: Workflow is like training for the agent. Without it, every run is a lottery.

instructions.0: Write steps as a numbered list.
instructions.1: Each step — a concrete action + what gets passed to the next.
instructions.2: The final step — output format for the parent agent.

ag-4.example:
## Workflow

1. Read `git diff` of current changes (or specified PR).
2. For each file in diff:
   a. Check security: input validation, secrets, injection.
   b. Check correctness: edge cases, off-by-one, null handling.
   c. Check readability: naming, complexity, dead code.
3. Group findings by severity:
   - 🔴 Critical (blocks merge)
   - 🟡 Important (should fix)
   - 🟢 Nit (optional)
4. Return markdown report:
   - Top: 1-line summary (status: clean / yellow / red)
   - Per-issue: file:line + what's wrong + how to fix.
5. NEVER rewrite code — only point out issues.
ag-4.validate: The workflow reads like a recipe: it's clear what the agent does at each step.
ag-4.tip: If there are > 8 steps — the agent is too big. Split it.

ag-5.title: Create the subagent in Claude Code
ag-5.why: The agent file lives in `.claude/agents/<name>.md`. This is simpler than it sounds.

instructions.0: In the project root: `mkdir -p .claude/agents`.
instructions.1: Create the file `.claude/agents/code-reviewer.md` with frontmatter (see example).
instructions.2: Restart `claude`.
instructions.3: In the chat ask: 'run code-reviewer on the current changes'.

ag-5.example:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Use when user asks to review code changes... [full description]
tools: Read, Bash
---

You are a senior code reviewer. Your job is to review code changes...

[full workflow from step 4]
ag-5.validate: The agent activates on the trigger and produces a structured report.

troubleshoot.Agent doesn't activate: Check the description — is it clear to Claude, not just to you? Tighten the triggers.
troubleshoot.Agent runs but output is wrong: Agentti toimii mutta tulos ei vastaa odotuksia
troubleshoot.Agent works but output is wrong: Tighten the workflow — especially the last step about the output format.

ag-6.title: Test and iterate on 5 real tasks
ag-6.why: Without testing the agent is a hypothesis. Real runs surface weak spots.

instructions.0: Run the agent 5 times on different real tasks.
instructions.1: Each time: what worked well, what didn't.
instructions.2: Weak spots — add rules to the workflow or anti-triggers to the description.
instructions.3: After 5–10 iterations the agent stabilizes.

ag-6.validate: You have a minimum of 5 real runs; improvements are recorded in the agent file.
ag-6.tip: The best agents are born through iteration, not from 'a brilliant first draft'. Don't worry about perfection.

intro.title: Your first Claude session
intro.subtitle: Open, ask, understand — the basics in one go
intro.whatItIs: The very first tutorial — before models, context, and prompts. What Claude is, how it differs from other AI tools, what to expect and what mistaken expectations to avoid. Suited for someone who has never heard of Claude before.
intro.approach: Don't try to write a complex prompt right away. Make 3 different requests (a question, a task, something creative) and see how Claude responds. Getting acquainted is about calibrating expectations, not achieving a result.

outcomes.0: Understand that Claude is a conversational AI model, not a search engine
outcomes.1: Know who Anthropic is and why they built Constitutional AI
outcomes.2: Distinguish Claude's strengths from its typical failures
outcomes.3: Have realistic expectations from the first conversation

0.title: First encounter
0.description: Opened claude.ai, typed 'hi' — now you know what to do next and what NOT to expect.

1.title: Making a decision
1.description: Whether to try Claude for your work at all — after this tutorial you have criteria.

2.title: Explaining to colleagues
2.description: You can tell someone what Claude is in 5 minutes, without fluff.

pitfalls.0: Expecting Claude to know 'everything' — it has a knowledge cutoff.
pitfalls.1: Treating the answer as fact — models sometimes confidently get things wrong.
pitfalls.2: Comparing to Google Search — these are different tools with different strengths.

0.question: Ask Claude in one sentence: 'What can you do and where are your limitations?'. Compare the answer to your expectations.
0.hint: A good answer — short and honest, no marketing. If you get 'I can do everything' — ask for specifics.

1.question: Ask 3 requests: a factual question, a creative task, a breakdown of a simple document. Compare the quality.
1.hint: You'll notice — Claude is strong at analysis and phrasing, weaker on fresh facts (without web search).

in-1.title: Open claude.ai in the browser
in-1.why: The very first entry point. Without an account you can't try anything.

instructions.0: Go to claude.ai.
instructions.1: Register via email or OAuth.
instructions.2: Close the onboarding pop-ups — we'll learn structurally.

in-2.title: Ask the first 'factual' question
in-2.why: This shows Claude's strong side — structured explanations.

instructions.0: Write: 'Explain in one paragraph what the HTTP protocol is and what it's for'.
instructions.1: Read the answer.
instructions.2: Notice: Claude answers structurally, without 'lyrical' preambles.

in-2.prompt: Explain in one paragraph what the HTTP protocol is and what it's for. No unnecessary details.
in-2.validate: You got a short, concrete answer — without a long opener.
in-2.tip: Claude is great at explanations. Use it as an 'on-demand teacher' on any topic.

in-3.title: Ask about 'today'
in-3.why: Now you'll see the limitation — the knowledge cutoff.

instructions.0: Write: 'What are the tech news from the past week?'.
instructions.1: Notice: Claude will say 'I don't know' or 'My knowledge cutoff is date X'.
instructions.2: This is fine — it's not a bug, it's a known property of the model.

in-3.prompt: What are the tech news from the past week?
in-3.validate: Claude explicitly mentions the cutoff or warns about outdated information.
in-3.tip: For 'fresh' info you need [[node:cap-search|web search]] (see the 'Capabilities' section).

in-4.title: Upload a file and discuss it

instructions.0: Drag a PDF or Word document into the chat (brand guide, article, report).
instructions.1: Write: 'Make a summary in 5 points'.
instructions.2: Read the answer. Notice — Claude cites specific parts of the document.

in-4.prompt: Make a summary of this document in 5 points by priority.
in-4.validate: The answer is tied to the specific content, not generic.

in-5.title: Compare with search
in-5.why: To calibrate expectations: where is Claude stronger, where is search.

instructions.0: Write down two cases from your work.
instructions.1: Think: which is better solved with Google, which with Claude.
instructions.2: Rule: Google — for facts and links. Claude — for analysis, synthesis, phrasing.

in-5.validate: You have a clear mental split: when you'll go to Google, when to Claude.
