prompting-techniques.title: Prompting techniques: hands-on
prompting-techniques.subtitle: Few-shot, CoT, XML, Prefill, Structured output — on one task
prompting-techniques.whatItIs: A workshop on 5 fundamental techniques that turn an 'average' prompt into a reliable tool. You apply each technique to the same task to see what each one affects.
prompting-techniques.approach: One baseline prompt → 5 versions with different techniques → comparison. Without comparison you won't feel the effect; with it — the techniques settle into muscle memory.

outcomes.0: Apply Few-shot, CoT, XML, Prefill consciously — to a specific problem
outcomes.1: Get JSON output that parses on the first try
outcomes.2: Know which technique helps with which prompt failure
outcomes.3: Can iteratively improve a prompt in 3–5 targeted steps

0.title: Exact format
0.description: If you need JSON/table/markdown — Prefill + Structured output technique.

1.title: Complex reasoning
1.description: Analytics, cause-and-effect chains — Chain of Thought.

2.title: Subtle style / tone
2.description: Brand voice, a specific report format — Few-shot examples.

pitfalls.0: Applying all 5 techniques at once — you won't know what helped. Use one at a time.
pitfalls.1: Giving contradictory few-shot examples — the model will pick a random pattern.
pitfalls.2: Prefilling a long starting text — the model stretches to reach it and loses quality. 1–3 anchor tokens is enough.
pitfalls.3: Asking for 'JSON' without a schema and example — Claude will invent the fields.

0.question: Take your baseline prompt and make 5 versions: +CoT, +Few-shot, +XML, +Prefill, +Structured. Compare results.
0.hint: Works best on a medium-difficulty task — a simple one will be solved by one technique; a very complex one won't be saved by five.

1.question: Find a task in your work routine where you currently manually parse Claude's answer. Rewrite the prompt using Structured output.
1.hint: Compare time 'prompt + manual parse' vs 'prompt + auto-parse'. Should be 5–10× savings.

2.question: Take a prompt that gives ~70% results. Make 3 iterations using 'one fix → check → next fix'.
2.hint: After each iteration write down: what improved, what broke.

pt-1.title: Lock in a baseline prompt
pt-1.why: Without a baseline you won't see what each technique improved.

instructions.0: Take a real task from your work (document audit / data analysis / text structuring).
instructions.1: Phrase the prompt in ONE line — the way you'd normally write in a chat.
instructions.2: Run in Sonnet, save the result as the baseline.

pt-1.prompt: Analyze this text and give conclusions.
pt-1.validate: You have a one-liner prompt + Claude's answer as the baseline.
pt-1.tip: The more 'average' the baseline quality — the more noticeable the technique's effect. A great baseline is already good; a terrible one — techniques won't save it.

pt-2.title: Apply Chain of Thought
pt-2.why: CoT (Chain-of-Thought — asking AI to «think out loud» step by step) gives +20–40% accuracy on tasks where you need to 'derive', not 'recall'.

instructions.0: Add to the baseline: 'Think step by step. First list the facts, then hypotheses, then conclusions.'
instructions.1: Run in a new chat on the same task.
instructions.2: Compare the reasoning depth with the baseline.

pt-2.prompt: Analyze this text. Think step by step: 1) list the facts 2) formulate 2–3 hypotheses 3) check each one 4) give a recommendation.
pt-2.validate: The answer contains explicit reasoning stages, not just the conclusion.
pt-2.tip: CoT is not needed for simple questions — just a longer answer. Use it where there's 'logic', not 'fact'.

pt-3.title: Add Few-shot examples
pt-3.why: Few-shot (a handful of examples in the prompt that AI mimics) is the most powerful technique for non-standard formats and tone.

instructions.0: Come up with 2 mini-examples: what input → what output you want.
instructions.1: Structure: 'Example 1: input: ... output: ... Example 2: ... Now do for: ...'
instructions.2: Run. Check — did the model reproduce the style of the examples?

pt-3.prompt:
Example 1: input: <short text> → output: <in your format>.
Example 2: input: <another text> → output: <in your format>.
Now do for: <your real input>.
pt-3.validate: Output follows the pattern of the examples, not its 'own'.
pt-3.tip: 2–3 examples are usually better than 5+ — more noise, not signal. Use varied examples.

troubleshoot.Model copies the example verbatim: The examples are too close to your input. Make them on-topic but not same-content.
troubleshoot.Ignores the example format: Add explicitly: 'Format — strictly as in the examples'.

pt-4.title: Structure with XML tags
pt-4.why: XML gives +2–3× stability on long prompts with different data types.

instructions.0: Split the prompt into blocks: <context>, <task>, <examples>, <constraints>.
instructions.1: Put each piece in its own tag. Text inside — plain.
instructions.2: Run. Notice — the model 'confuses' data and instructions less.

pt-4.prompt:
<context>...</context>
<task>Analyze the text from <input></task>
<input>...</input>
<constraints>English only. No introductory phrases. Maximum 5 points.</constraints>
pt-4.validate: The prompt reads as a structure, not a 'wall of text'. The model clearly separates data from instructions.
pt-4.tip: XML is for long prompts with different blocks. On a short request — overkill.

pt-5.title: Lock in format via Prefill
pt-5.why: Prefill (starting AI's response for it to lock tone/format) firmly sets the start of the answer — the model doesn't 'drift' from the format.

instructions.0: In the chat — write: 'Start the answer exactly with <YOUR_ANCHOR>'.
instructions.1: Anchor = the first character of the needed format: { for JSON, | for a table, # for a markdown heading.
instructions.2: Run. The model 'jumps' straight into the format.

pt-5.prompt: <your request>. Start the answer exactly with | (this is a markdown table). No preamble.
pt-5.validate: The answer starts with your anchor, without 'Sure, here is...' openers.
pt-5.tip: In the API, prefill goes as a role: 'assistant' message at the end of messages — the model continues from it.

pt-6.title: Get JSON via Structured output
pt-6.why: The final technique — turns the answer into parseable JSON.

instructions.0: Describe the JSON schema explicitly: which fields, which types, which enum values.
instructions.1: Give a mini-example of valid output.
instructions.2: Close with a Prefill on `{`.
instructions.3: Run through JSON.parse() — should work on the first try.

pt-6.validate: JSON parses on the first try. Fields match the schema.
pt-6.tip: If the model adds ```json — prefill didn't work. Strengthen: 'WITHOUT markdown wrapper. Raw JSON only'.

troubleshoot.Fields sometimes missing: Add 'all fields are required' to the schema. Don't rely on 'the model will figure it out'.
troubleshoot.Fields with extra garbage: Show a bad and good example: 'don't do this: ...; do this: ...'.

pt-7.title: Iteration: one failure — one fix
pt-7.why: A method for improving a prompt without rewriting from scratch.

instructions.0: Take a prompt that gives ~70%.
instructions.1: Find ONE specific failure (e.g., 'the output is too generic').
instructions.2: Make ONE change (role / constraint / example).
instructions.3: Run on 2–3 different inputs. Record: helped / didn't.

pt-7.validate: You have v4 vs v1 of the prompt — a noticeable difference without a full rewrite.
pt-7.tip: Change 5 things at once — you won't know what helped. One step = one hypothesis.

subagents.title: Subagents in Claude Code
subagents.subtitle: Parallel agents — Explore, Plan, your own custom ones
subagents.whatItIs: A subagent is an isolated executor inside [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]]: its own context, its own tools, its own output. This is NOT a Skill (Skill = knowledge-of-how-to-do; Subagent = who-does-it). After this workshop the confusion disappears.
subagents.approach: First use the built-in subagents (Explore, Plan) on a real task — to understand what 'context isolation' means. Only then create your own. Without this order your own will be an 'under-Skill'.

outcomes.0: Run Explore to search a large repo without bloating the context
outcomes.1: Run Plan before dangerous changes
outcomes.2: Create your own custom subagent for a team routine task
outcomes.3: Know when a subagent beats a Skill (and vice versa)

0.title: Search through a large repo
0.description: Run Explore — it returns findings; your main context stays clean.

1.title: Dangerous edits
1.description: A planned refactor of 20+ files — Plan builds a plan, you review it, then apply.

2.title: Team
2.description: Your own code-reviewer, security-auditor — set up once, the whole team uses it consistently.

pitfalls.0: Using a subagent for a simple task (read 2 files) — overkill, you lose speed.
pitfalls.1: Creating your own subagent without a clear trigger in the description — it will never activate.
pitfalls.2: Giving a subagent a prompt like 'continue my reasoning' — it doesn't see your history; it needs a complete brief.
pitfalls.3: Making a subagent for 'parallelism' where tasks depend on each other — you'll get conflicting results.

0.question: Run Explore on your work repo: 'Find all places where deprecated API X is used'. Compare the time with a manual grep.
0.hint: Explore should return a structured list — not 'here are a few places', but a complete one.

1.question: Create your own subagent for a recurring task (code review / changelog / dependency audit). Run it on a real branch.
1.hint: Description = trigger. 'Use when user asks for X'. Not 'does X'.

2.question: Find a task you used to do with a Skill. Reformulate it as a subagent. Measure — where is the gain, where is the loss.
2.hint: Subagent wins on long searches; Skill wins on short reproducible procedures.

sa-1.title: Launch Claude Code in the repo
sa-1.why: Subagents are only in Claude Code, not in [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]]. You need an install + a project.

instructions.0: Open the terminal in the repo: cd ~/projects/your-repo
instructions.1: Run: claude
instructions.2: If first time — go through /init for CLAUDE.md.

sa-1.validate: You see the Claude Code prompt in the terminal. Session is active.

troubleshoot.Starts but no files: You're not in a git repository. Navigate to a real project.

sa-2.title: View the available subagents
sa-2.why: First — reconnaissance. What comes out of the box.

instructions.0: In the chat type: /agents
instructions.1: Read the list: Explore (search), Plan (planning), general-purpose.
instructions.2: Notice: each has a description and tools.

sa-2.validate: You have a list of 3+ subagents with descriptions.
sa-2.tip: If plugins are installed — subagents are added. That's normal.

sa-3.title: Run Explore on a real task
sa-3.why: This is the key moment — you'll understand what 'context isolation' means.

instructions.0: Phrase the task: 'Where is deprecated X used?' or 'Find all TODOs about Y'.
instructions.1: Ask: 'Run the Explore agent for searching ...' — Claude delegates itself.
instructions.2: Wait for the result — it comes as a summary, not a raw search log.
instructions.3: Check: your main context didn't inflate with files — only findings are there.

sa-3.prompt: Use the Explore agent: find all places in the repo where deprecated X is imported, and return the list with file:line.
sa-3.validate: You get a clean list 'file:line — what was found' in the main chat, without raw grep output.
sa-3.tip: If the task requires reading 5+ files — that's unambiguously Explore. If 1–2 — regular Read is faster.

sa-4.title: Run Plan before a dangerous change
sa-4.why: Plan is 'think before you act', without editing files.

instructions.0: Phrase the task: 'Rewrite all handlers of X in the style of Y'.
instructions.1: Ask: 'First run the Plan agent' — Claude returns a plan as a list of changes.
instructions.2: Read the plan critically. Find risks / omissions.
instructions.3: Approve the plan or go back to refine — then run the implementation.

sa-4.prompt: Run the Plan agent for refactoring <specific location>. I want to see the list of files, changes, and potential regressions before any edits.
sa-4.validate: You have a plan with specific file:line entries and change descriptions, WITHOUT applied changes.
sa-4.tip: Plan + manual plan review = 5× fewer 'oops' on large changes. Especially valuable on legacy.

sa-5.title: Create your own custom subagent
sa-5.why: Your own turns a regular task into a button.

instructions.0: In the chat: /agents → create new.
instructions.1: Name: e.g., security-reviewer.
instructions.2: Description: 'Use when user asks to review security of changes / PR / branch' (trigger!).
instructions.3: Steps: 1) read git diff, 2) check OWASP top-10, 3) output as a severity-ranked list.

sa-5.validate: The new agent is visible in /agents. The config is in .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md.
sa-5.tip: Description is MORE IMPORTANT than the name. Without a clear trigger the agent will never activate.

troubleshoot.Agent doesn't start on 'do a security re: Description is too generic or conflicts with another agent. Make it unique.
troubleshoot.Starts on irrelevant requests: Description is too broad. Add negative triggers: 'Use ONLY when ...'.

sa-6.title: Understand the Skill vs Subagent difference
sa-6.why: The final lock-in. Without it the confusion will return in a week.

instructions.0: Take 3 of your recurring tasks.
instructions.1: For each answer: is context isolation needed? Are custom tools needed? Is the task long?
instructions.2: All 'yes' → subagent. All 'no' → Skill. Mixed → think more.
instructions.3: Record the choice in a table: Task → Skill | Subagent | Hybrid.

sa-6.validate: You have 3 tasks with a justified tool choice. You can explain the choice in words.
sa-6.tip: Hybrid is also possible: a Skill invokes a Subagent for the heavy part — best of both worlds.

subagents.trigger: You're confused: how is a Skill different from a Subagent — and when to use which.

tool-use.title: Tool use: give Claude hands
tool-use.subtitle: Function calling — the foundation of integrations, agents and MCP
tool-use.whatItIs: [[node:cap-tools|Tool use]] (function calling) is the mechanism through which Claude calls your functions via a JSON schema. It's the basis of MCP, custom agents, and any integrations. After this workshop you understand the architecture from the inside, not as 'magic'.
tool-use.approach: Without good tool descriptions the agent will constantly make mistakes. First learn to write descriptions, then design tool sets. The actual call code is secondary — the SDK writes it.

outcomes.0: Understand the tool use flow: schema → tool selection → call → result → answer
outcomes.1: Describe a tool so Claude picks the right one 95% of the time
outcomes.2: Know when tool use beats MCP and when it's the reverse
outcomes.3: Competently design a tool set for your agent

0.title: Your own agent
0.description: Any custom agent = a system of tools. Without understanding tool use you can't build an agent.

1.title: Product integration
1.description: Claude in your app calling functions from your backend — that's tool use.

2.title: MCP architecture
2.description: An MCP server = just tools on a standard protocol. Understand tool use, you understand MCP.

pitfalls.0: Providing tools without a clear description of effects — Claude will call a destructive one with the wrong arguments.
pitfalls.1: Making a 'universal' tool with 10 parameters instead of 3 narrow ones — Claude gets confused.
pitfalls.2: Not separating read and write tools — the model mixes queries and changes.
pitfalls.3: Relying on 'the model will figure out' the parameter types — describe JSON Schema strictly.

0.question: Take a task from work (e.g., 'respond to support tickets'). Design 3–5 tools for an agent: names, parameters, effects.
0.hint: Separate read (get_ticket, list_recent) and write (reply, escalate). Each — narrow.

1.question: Take one tool from your project and write 2 versions of the description: bad (1 phrase) and good (what, when, what NOT to do). Compare Claude's choices.
1.hint: Good description = when to apply + when not to apply + example arguments.

2.question: Find a process in your work where you currently use free chat. Design how it would look through tool use.
2.hint: If the task = 'find and do' — that's an ideal tool use candidate.

tu-1.title: Understand tool use in plain terms
tu-1.why: Without an interaction model the next steps are someone else's kitchen.

instructions.0: Read the flow schema: User → Claude → Claude picks a tool → your system executes → result → Claude forms the answer.
instructions.1: Notice: Claude does NOT execute code. It only decides 'which tool to call and with what arguments'.
instructions.2: Execution is on your side (SDK / MCP-server / your backend).

tu-1.validate: You can explain in 30 seconds: who does what in the tool use flow.
tu-1.tip: This is exactly the same pattern as MCP — it's a standardized transport between Claude and tools.

tu-2.title: Read the minimal JSON tool schema
tu-2.why: This is the format Claude sees. Mastering it is mandatory.

instructions.0: Open the example: name + description + input_schema (JSON Schema).
instructions.1: Notice: input_schema describes parameters via type, description, enum, required.
instructions.2: Description is the most important part. Claude reads it to decide 'apply or not'.
instructions.3: Example: name: "get_weather", description: "Get current weather for a city. Use ONLY when user asks about current weather, not forecasts.", input_schema: { city: { type: "string" } }.

tu-2.validate: You can write a schema from scratch for a tool 'send email' — name, description, parameters.
tu-2.tip: Anthropic SDK / MCP / [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] — all use the same schema. Learn once — apply everywhere.

tu-3.title: Write a good description
tu-3.why: The most common reason 'the agent doesn't work' — a bad description.

instructions.0: Template: WHAT it does (1 phrase) → WHEN to apply (trigger) → WHEN NOT to apply (anti-trigger) → EXAMPLE arguments.
instructions.1: Take your tool from exercise 2. Write the description using the template.
instructions.2: Test: give 3 different user requests — Claude should correctly decide whether to use the tool.

tu-3.prompt: description: "Send transactional email to a user (e.g. order confirmation, password reset). Use when user explicitly asks to notify a person. Do NOT use for marketing emails — those go through marketing_send. Example args: {to: \"user@x.com\", template: \"order-confirmed\", vars: {order_id: \"42\"}}"
tu-3.validate: Description contains when to apply + anti-trigger + example.
tu-3.tip: One paragraph of description often = the difference between 60% accuracy and 95%. Don't skimp.

tu-4.title: Design a narrow tool set
tu-4.why: Narrow tools = reliable agent. Broad = confusion.

instructions.0: Take the task from exercise 1. Split into read / write tools.
instructions.1: Each tool — one goal, no more than 3–5 parameters.
instructions.2: Dangerous actions (write / delete) — separate tools with an explicit confirm flag.
instructions.3: No more than 10 tools per agent. If more — split into two agents.

tu-4.validate: You have 3–7 tools, each narrow, read and write separated, dangerous ones separate.
tu-4.tip: Good sign: you can say about each tool 'when I would use it'. If you struggle — it's either redundant or poorly described.

troubleshoot.Got 15 tools: Some are redundant. Merge similar ones (if parameters align) or split the agent in two.
troubleshoot.One tool with 8 parameters: Split into 2–3 narrow ones — Claude will choose more precisely.

tu-5.title: Decide: tool use vs MCP
tu-5.why: When to write it yourself, when to use MCP.

instructions.0: Direct tool use = when tools are specific to your product, nobody else needs them.
instructions.1: MCP = when tools can be useful to multiple clients / reusable / standardization is needed.
instructions.2: Compare: is your task reusable? If yes — MCP. If unique — regular tool use.

tu-5.validate: You understand when you build an MCP server, when you just add tools for your own agent.
tu-5.tip: Company-internal CRM = tool use (nobody outside the company uses it). Postgres wrapper = MCP (universally useful).

tu-6.title: Apply to your own task
tu-6.why: Without applying this — it's all theory.

instructions.0: Take one process from work that you repeat >5 times a week.
instructions.1: Describe it as 2–3 tools (or MCP server) on paper / in Notion.
instructions.2: Don't write code — write a spec: name, description, params.

tu-6.validate: You have a specification for a real process. Ready to hand off to a developer / implement yourself.
tu-6.tip: A specification is more valuable than 'I tried to code it' — without one the code will be rewritten 3 times.

tool-use.trigger: You need Claude to call your functions / API — not just produce text.
inputs: Description of the function to call
outputs: Working tool_use loop with JSON schema
Understanding of ToolResult and error handling
Foundation for MCP / agents / integrations
tool-use.savings: ~80% integration time vs hand-parsing text responses

hooks.title: Hooks: automating discipline
hooks.subtitle: Guaranteed actions on events — no more 'I hope it won't forget'
hooks.whatItIs: Hooks are shell commands that [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]] executes on events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, etc.). They run AT THE HARNESS LEVEL, not the model level. So they're reliable: the model cannot 'forget' a hook.
hooks.approach: Hooks are code, not text. First understand events and environment variables, then write your first hook on a safe action (file formatting). Only then — on sensitive ones (deny on rm -rf).

outcomes.0: Know all the key events (Pre/Post ToolUse, Stop, UserPromptSubmit)
outcomes.1: Set up 2–3 working hooks: auto-format, guard on dangerous commands, post-edit checks
outcomes.2: Understand the difference: hook vs slash-command vs subagent
outcomes.3: Can share hooks with the team via settings.json in git

0.title: Code quality
0.description: PostToolUse:Write → prettier / linter. Guaranteed format on every edit.

1.title: Security
1.description: PreToolUse:Bash → block dangerous commands (rm -rf, git push --force) before execution.

2.title: Metrics / observability
2.description: Stop → log the session to jsonl. See what Claude did and how many tokens it spent.

pitfalls.0: A heavy shell script in a hook — slows every Claude action. A hook must be fast (<500ms).
pitfalls.1: A hook that edits the same file — can get into an infinite loop with the model. Use PostToolUse:Write carefully.
pitfalls.2: Putting hooks with secrets in the shared settings.json — they end up in git. Sensitive ones go in settings.local.json.
pitfalls.3: Using a hook instead of a subagent for long tasks — a hook blocks. Long tasks → subagent.

0.question: Find a 'after every edit of X — do Y' task in your workflow. Implement it as a PostToolUse hook.
0.hint: Classics: prettier after Write, npm test after Edit on a test file, git status after Bash.

1.question: Find a dangerous command you don't trust Claude with. Make a PreToolUse hook that blocks it.
1.hint: Template: check $CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND via grep -E for the pattern → exit 1 on match.

2.question: Make a Stop hook that logs the session end to .claude/logs/session.jsonl. Use for analytics on 'what I worked on'.

hk-1.title: Understand the event model
hk-1.why: Hooks are tied to events. Know the events — know the possibilities.

instructions.0: Key ones: PreToolUse (before a tool call — can cancel), PostToolUse (after — can react).
instructions.1: Useful: Stop (session end), UserPromptSubmit (new user prompt).
instructions.2: Each event provides environment variables: $CLAUDE_FILE_PATH, $CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND, $CLAUDE_TOOL_NAME.

hk-1.validate: You can name 3 events and for each — a typical use scenario.
hk-1.tip: Pre vs Post — a common source of confusion. Pre = before, you can block. Post = after, you can react.

hk-2.title: Open settings.json and find the hooks section

instructions.0: Open .claude/settings.json in the repo. If it doesn't exist — create it.
instructions.1: Find or add the section: "hooks": { ... }.
instructions.2: Under each event — an array of commands: "PostToolUse:Write": [{"command": "..."}].

hk-2.validate: You have valid JSON with an empty hooks block.
hk-2.tip: Hooks in settings.json go into git. In settings.local.json — local only. Choose consciously.

hk-3.title: Write your first hook — auto-format

instructions.0: Add: "PostToolUse:Write": [{"command": "npx prettier --write $CLAUDE_FILE_PATH 2>/dev/null || true"}].
instructions.1: Restart Claude Code to pick up the settings.
instructions.2: Ask Claude to edit a file. After the Write — you'll see that prettier ran.
instructions.3: || true at the end — so the hook doesn't fail if the file isn't supported by prettier.

hk-3.validate: After any Claude edit — the file is automatically formatted.
hk-3.tip: The same template works for biome, eslint --fix, ruff format — any formatters.

troubleshoot.Hook doesn't fire: Check: did you restart Claude? The filename must match the prettier pattern.
troubleshoot.Claude hangs after Write: The hook is too slow. Add a timeout or move to background.

hk-4.title: Protect yourself from dangerous commands with a PreToolUse hook
hk-4.why: A real guard. Especially important if you've allowed Bash in permissions.

instructions.0: Add: "PreToolUse:Bash": [{"command": "echo \"$CLAUDE_BASH_COMMAND\" | grep -qE \"rm -rf|git push --force|git reset --hard\" && exit 1 || exit 0"}].
instructions.1: Restart Claude. Ask Claude to run rm -rf temp/.
instructions.2: The hook should block — Claude gets an error and doesn't run the command.

hk-4.validate: The dangerous command is blocked before execution; a safe command passes.
hk-4.tip: This is deny-by-pattern, complementing permissions.deny. Useful when permissions are too broad.

hk-5.title: Log the session via a Stop hook

instructions.0: Add: "Stop": [{"command": "echo \"$(date +%s),$CLAUDE_SESSION_ID,$CLAUDE_TOTAL_TOKENS\" >> .claude/logs/session.csv"}].
instructions.1: mkdir -p .claude/logs.
instructions.2: Work with Claude. Close the session.
instructions.3: Open .claude/logs/session.csv — your stats are there.

hk-5.validate: Sessions are logged with timestamp + tokens.
hk-5.tip: Over the long run, these stats will show which tasks are expensive and which are cheap. Useful for optimization.

hk-6.title: Decide: hook vs slash vs subagent

instructions.0: Hook — on an event, synchronous, fast (<500ms), no decision logic.
instructions.1: Slash command — on a user trigger, can be long-running.
instructions.2: Subagent — a parallel task with context isolation.
instructions.3: Take 3 of your needs → choose a tool for each.

hk-6.validate: You can justify the choice for 3 tasks — why specifically hook / slash / subagent.
hk-6.tip: Hooks are especially valuable for guaranteed actions — the model might 'forget', a hook won't.

hooks.trigger: Claude Code sometimes «forgets» to run tests/lint before a commit — you need hard discipline.
inputs: List of events to intercept (PreToolUse, Stop, ...)
outputs: Working hooks config in settings.json
Automatic lint/test/format on the right events
Guarantee the model can't «forget»
hooks.savings: ~20-30 min/day on manual checks + zero «forgotten» tests

first-project.title: Create your first project with Claude
first-project.subtitle: From an empty computer to Claude Code running
first-project.whatItIs: An end-to-end tutorial for the absolute beginner: install Node.js, open the terminal, create a folder, install [[node:claude-code|Claude Code]], run the first [[node:cc-cmd-init|/init]] and send the first real prompt. No assumption that "you already know cd".
first-project.approach: The tutorial branches at step 1: [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]] (no terminal, you finish at step 2) or Claude Code (everything through step 10). Pick by what matters: a quick start without installs, or full control over the project files.

outcomes.0: Understand the difference between a claude.ai Project and a local folder
outcomes.1: Installed Node.js and can check the version
outcomes.2: Opened the terminal and don't fear it
outcomes.3: Created your first working folder (two ways)
outcomes.4: Installed Claude Code and completed authentication
outcomes.5: Generated CLAUDE.md and sent your first real prompt

0.title: First day with Claude
0.description: Replaces "I read the docs and nothing works" with "in 30 minutes I'm already doing things".

1.title: Onboarding a coworker
1.description: Share the link — and a colleague reaches the same starting state as you in half an hour.

2.title: Clean install
2.description: Got a new Mac or switched to Windows — run the tutorial and rebuild your work environment.

pitfalls.0: Skipping step 1 (choosing the path) and rushing into the terminal — only to realize a claude.ai Project would have been enough.
pitfalls.1: Creating a folder with spaces or non-ASCII in the name — then cd complains and you don't know why.
pitfalls.2: Installing an old Node.js (<18) — Claude Code will complain "engine not supported".
pitfalls.3: Skipping /init — Claude re-discovers the project every time.

0.question: Walk the tutorial to the end along the path you chose at step 1. Time yourself.
0.hint: Path A (claude.ai) — 5–10 min. Path B (Claude Code) — 25–35 min.

1.question: After finishing — create a second folder for a second project and verify that Claude Code picks up a different CLAUDE.md correctly.
1.hint: This checks you understood isolation: one project = one folder = its own context.

fp-1.title: Choose your path: claude.ai or Claude Code
fp-1.why: These are two different ways to work with Claude, both valid. Better to choose now than redo it an hour later.

instructions.0: claude.ai (path A): browser chat, Projects, Artifacts. No terminal. No install. Enough for most tasks: writing, analysis, discussion.
instructions.1: Claude Code (path B): a CLI tool that works with your local files, uses git and MCP. Needs a terminal and Node.js. For development and automation.
instructions.2: Rule of thumb: if your task is "discuss a document" — path A is enough. If it's "edit code in a repo" — path B.
instructions.3: Pick a path and commit: A → go to step 2 and finish. B → go to step 3 and the rest of the tutorial.

fp-1.validate: You can explain to yourself in one sentence why you picked this path.
fp-1.tip: Unsure — start with A. Moving to B later is no harder than now.

fp-2.title: Path A — create a Project in claude.ai
fp-2.why: A Project is your persistent workspace in claude.ai with its own instructions and knowledge base. This is the final step of the short path.

instructions.0: Open claude.ai → sign in (Free is enough to start, Pro is needed for Projects).
instructions.1: In the left sidebar find "Projects" → "+ New project".
instructions.2: Name: what you do + for what (e.g., "Regular report audit").
instructions.3: Description: 1–2 lines — what this project is for and what result you expect.
instructions.4: Upload 1–3 files into Project knowledge (if you have any). That's enough to start.
instructions.5: Done. Open the first chat in the Project and send a real prompt.

fp-2.prompt: Using the uploaded files from Project knowledge, do the first analysis for the input: [URL / document / description]. Format — top-5 observations by priority.
fp-2.validate: You have a Project with at least one real chat, and Claude's answer is concrete and references the uploaded files.
fp-2.tip: If you want to continue along path B later — go to step 3. The knowledge won't be lost.

troubleshoot.No Projects section: This is a Pro feature. Free plan hides it. Either upgrade to Pro or work in regular chats without a Project.
troubleshoot.I don't see \"New project\": You may have a free Team tier. Check your subscription in the top-right.

fp-3.title: Path B — install Node.js
fp-3.why: Node.js is required to run npm packages, including Claude Code. Without it nothing will install.

instructions.0: macOS (recommended): open Terminal.app (Cmd+Space → "Terminal" → Enter) and run `brew install node`. If brew isn't installed — install it first from brew.sh.
instructions.1: macOS (alternative): download the installer from nodejs.org → run the .pkg → follow the steps.
instructions.2: Windows: download the installer from nodejs.org → run the .msi → tick "Add to PATH" → restart PowerShell.
instructions.3: Verify: in the terminal run `node -v`. It should print a version like v20.11.0 or newer.

fp-3.tip: Version 20 or 22 LTS is optimal. 14 or 16 is old and may have issues with Claude Code.

troubleshoot.command not found: node: The terminal doesn't see the install. Close and reopen it. On Windows — make sure you ticked "Add to PATH" in the installer.
troubleshoot.command not found: brew (mac): Brew isn't installed. Open brew.sh, copy the install command, paste into the terminal, run it. Takes 5 minutes.

fp-4.title: Open the terminal and figure out where you are
fp-4.why: The terminal is the workspace for Claude Code. It's worth seeing what it even looks like and getting over the fear.

instructions.0: macOS: Cmd+Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. A black (or white) window with a cursor opens.
instructions.1: Windows: open the Start menu → type "PowerShell" or "Windows Terminal" → Enter.
instructions.2: In the terminal type `pwd` (mac) or `pwd` / `echo %cd%` (Windows) → press Enter. It shows where you are.
instructions.3: Usually this is your home folder: /Users/name (mac) or C:\\Users\\name (Windows). That's normal.

fp-4.validate: Terminal is open, `pwd` prints the path to your home folder.
fp-4.tip: The "black screen" does nothing scary on its own. Only specific commands (rm -rf and similar) are dangerous, and you won't type them in this tutorial.

fp-5.title: Create a working folder
fp-5.why: A folder is the "home" of your project. Without one, files will pile up wherever.

instructions.0: Decision: where all your projects will live. I recommend `~/projects/` in home.
instructions.1: In the terminal: `mkdir -p ~/projects/my-first-claude-project` — creates the folder (and the parent `projects/` if it didn't exist).
instructions.2: Alternative via Finder/Explorer: open home → create a `projects` folder → inside it another one `my-first-claude-project`.
instructions.3: Name — ASCII only, no spaces. Use hyphens or underscores instead of spaces.

fp-5.validate: The folder exists. Verify: `ls ~/projects/` (mac) or `dir %USERPROFILE%\\projects\\` (Windows) — you'll see `my-first-claude-project` in the list.
fp-5.tip: The project name is easy to change later — it's just a folder. The key things are ASCII and no spaces.

troubleshoot.permission denied: You're trying to create a folder where you don't have rights. ~/ (home) is always yours. Don't create folders in /Applications or /System.
troubleshoot.mkdir: -p: command not found: Most likely you're on Windows using cmd.exe (old), not PowerShell. Switch to PowerShell or use `mkdir my-first-claude-project` without `-p`.

fp-6.title: Enter the folder and verify yourself
fp-6.why: Claude Code operates in the folder where you launched it. If you're not in the right one, Claude will see the wrong files.

instructions.0: In the terminal: `cd ~/projects/my-first-claude-project`.
instructions.1: Check: `pwd` → should print /Users/.../projects/my-first-claude-project.
instructions.2: Check what's inside: `ls` (mac) or `dir` (Windows). The folder is empty — that's normal for a new project.
instructions.3: Memorize `cd ~/projects/my-first-claude-project` — you'll use it every time you start working.

fp-6.validate: `pwd` prints the path to the new folder. You're in it.
fp-6.tip: `cd ..` — go up one level. `cd ~` — return home. That's the whole navigation vocabulary.

fp-7.title: Install Claude Code
fp-7.why: Claude Code is Claude's "hands" in your terminal. After install the `claude` command is available everywhere.

instructions.0: In the terminal (any folder): `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`.
instructions.1: Wait 30–60 seconds. npm will download and install the package globally.
instructions.2: Verify: `claude --version` → it should print the version number with no errors.
instructions.3: If you get EACCES — on mac/Linux run with sudo: `sudo npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`.

troubleshoot.EACCES permission denied: On mac/Linux — permissions are needed. Either `sudo npm install -g ...`, or configure npm prefix into your own folder (~/.npm-global) — google "npm permission EACCES".
troubleshoot.EEXIST file already exists: An old version is installed. `npm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, then install again.

fp-8.title: Launch claude and complete authentication
fp-8.why: First launch is short: you authenticate once via the browser, after that Claude Code remembers you.

instructions.0: Make sure you're in your working folder: `pwd` → my-first-claude-project.
instructions.1: Run: `claude`.
instructions.2: A browser opens with Anthropic auth → sign in with the same account as in claude.ai.
instructions.3: Return to the terminal. You'll see Claude Code's interactive prompt — you can type messages.

fp-8.validate: The terminal shows Claude Code's input field. The session is active.
fp-8.tip: If you accidentally closed the session — just run `claude` again from the same folder. The session's context isn't preserved, but [[node:cc-md|CLAUDE.md]] (if you have one) is picked up on the next launch.

troubleshoot.Browser doesn't open: Copy the URL from the terminal manually and open it in the browser.

fp-9.title: Create CLAUDE.md via /init
fp-9.why: CLAUDE.md is the project's "character". Claude reads it on every launch so it doesn't ask the same questions.

instructions.0: In the Claude session run: `/init`.
instructions.1: Claude scans the folder (it's empty right now — that's fine) and suggests a CLAUDE.md draft.
instructions.2: Read the draft. Remove what doesn't fit. Add rules — e.g., "I'm not a developer, explain in plain words", or "This project is about regular report audits".
instructions.3: Save the file (Ctrl+S or :wq in Vim, depending on your editor).

fp-9.validate: A CLAUDE.md file appeared in the project folder with your custom rules. Run `ls` (mac) or `dir` (Windows) — you'll see it.
fp-9.tip: Don't try to make a perfect CLAUDE.md on the first try. It's a living document — you'll keep extending it as you go.

troubleshoot./init doesn't work: You may have typed it in a regular claude.ai chat, not Claude Code. /init is a Claude Code slash command. Make sure you're in the terminal session.

fp-10.title: First real prompt on your own context
fp-10.why: Without a real prompt all of this is just an exercise. This is what the whole tutorial was for.

instructions.0: Think: what real task would you delegate to Claude right now? E.g., "help me structure my notes", "let's analyze this document", "sketch a plan for project X".
instructions.1: Phrase the request in the "Role → Task → Format" style (if you don't remember — do the basics tutorial afterward).
instructions.2: Send it to Claude Code. Read the answer.
instructions.3: If Claude wants to create a file — allow it. That's normal in your working folder.

fp-10.prompt: I'm working on <your context>. Help me <specific task> in <markdown / list / table> format. If you need inputs — ask questions.
fp-10.validate: Claude gave a meaningful answer tied to your context. Possibly created a file in the project folder.
fp-10.tip: Next learning steps: the basics tutorial — for theory of models and context, the claude-code tutorial — for deeper /security-review, hooks, subagents.

A simple project idea (landing, script, notes)

First real feature shipped by Claude's hands

tt-1.title: pwd — find out where you are now
tt-1.why: The terminal is always "inside" some folder. Finding out which is the first command of the day.

instructions.0: Open the terminal (if it isn't already): macOS Cmd+Space → "Terminal"; Windows — PowerShell.
instructions.1: Type: `pwd` (mac/linux/PowerShell) → press Enter.
instructions.2: Look at the output. That's the path to the folder you're in right now.

tt-1.example:
Mac: /Users/denisa
Windows: C:\Users\denisa
Usually when the terminal starts you're in your home — that's normal.
tt-1.validate: You see a line like /Users/<name> (mac) or C:\Users\<name> (Windows).
tt-1.tip: pwd = "print working directory". The simpler the command, the more often you use it. This one — literally every time.

tt-2.title: ls / dir — look at what's around
tt-2.why: Without ls you're flying blind. ls shows what folders and files are in the current one.

instructions.0: macOS / Linux: type `ls` → Enter.
instructions.1: Windows (PowerShell): `ls` works too. Old cmd.exe — `dir`.
instructions.2: Look at the list. That's the contents of your home folder: Documents, Downloads, Desktop, etc.

tt-2.example:
Mac/Linux output:
Applications  Desktop  Documents  Downloads  Movies  Music  Pictures  projects  Public

Windows output (dir):
  <DIR>  Documents
  <DIR>  Downloads
  ...
tt-2.validate: You see a list of folders: at least Desktop, Documents, Downloads.
tt-2.tip: `ls -la` (mac) shows hidden files (starting with .) and details. Useful later when you're looking for the .claude/ folder.

tt-3.title: mkdir + cd — create a folder and enter it
tt-3.why: That's the entire "start a new project" toolkit: create a folder → enter it.

instructions.0: Create a test folder: `mkdir tutorial-sandbox` → Enter.
instructions.1: Check it appeared: `ls` → it should be in the list.
instructions.2: Enter it: `cd tutorial-sandbox` → Enter.
instructions.3: Verify you're inside: `pwd` → should end with /tutorial-sandbox.

tt-3.validate: pwd prints a path ending with /tutorial-sandbox. Folder created, you're in it.
tt-3.tip: Tab is your best friend. Start typing `cd tut` → press Tab → the terminal completes to `cd tutorial-sandbox/`. Saves 90% of typing.

tt-4.title: cd .. and cd ~ — navigate back
tt-4.why: Knowing how to go back is as important as going in. Insurance against "where did I end up?".

instructions.0: You're now in tutorial-sandbox. Type `cd ..` → Enter. (Two dots = "folder above".)
instructions.1: Check: `pwd` → you're back in home.
instructions.2: Now go back in: `cd tutorial-sandbox` → verify pwd.
instructions.3: From anywhere you can return home with one command: `cd ~` (or just `cd`).

tt-4.validate: You understand: `..` = up one level, `~` = home, any path = a specific place.
tt-4.tip: On Windows the tilde (~) also works in PowerShell. `cd` with no arguments always returns home.

tt-5.title: Lock it in — a nested structure in one command
tt-5.why: Real task: create ~/projects/<name>/notes/ in one go. `mkdir -p` can do it.

instructions.0: From anywhere type: `mkdir -p ~/projects/my-first-project/notes` → Enter.
instructions.1: Enter it: `cd ~/projects/my-first-project` → check `ls` (you should see the notes folder).
instructions.2: You can delete the test: `cd ~` → then `rm -r tutorial-sandbox` (Mac/Linux) or `Remove-Item -Recurse tutorial-sandbox` (PowerShell). This removes the folder permanently.
instructions.3: Don't delete ~/projects/my-first-project — it'll come in handy in the first-project tutorial.

tt-5.validate: You see the notes folder inside ~/projects/my-first-project. Structure created in one command.
tt-5.tip: -p (parents) is a super useful flag. Without it, mkdir fails if the parent folder doesn't exist. With it — creates the whole chain.

troubleshoot.rm doesn't work on Windows: Windows uses `del` or `rmdir /s`. PowerShell handles `Remove-Item -Recurse`. When in doubt — delete via Explorer.
troubleshoot.Tab completion doesn't work: Normal for cmd.exe. Switch to PowerShell or Windows Terminal — autocomplete works there.

folders-workshop.title: Folders workshop: 3 structure examples
folders-workshop.subtitle: Audits, notes, experiment — build structure for three real cases
folders-workshop.whatItIs: Want to create folders with clicks in Finder/Explorer, or with a command in the terminal — your choice. This tutorial shows both ways across three live scenarios: work reports, personal notes, a throwaway experiment.
folders-workshop.approach: Don't pick ONE way. Create every folder both ways — via Finder AND via mkdir. After 3 rounds, your preference becomes deliberate.

outcomes.0: Create folders via both UI and terminal
outcomes.1: Know which names won't cause problems
outcomes.2: Understand how to organize the project tree meaningfully
outcomes.3: Can cleanly delete temporary experiments

0.title: Every new project
0.description: First step — a folder with a meaningful name in ~/projects/. Otherwise — chaos in a month.

1.title: Personal knowledge base
1.description: A separate hierarchy for notes, learning, recipes — kept apart from work folders.

2.title: Experiment / sandbox
2.description: A "trash" folder you're not afraid to delete. Every professional has one.

pitfalls.0: Spaces and non-ASCII in names — the terminal and git don't like them. "my project" ❌ → "my-project" ✅.
pitfalls.1: Folders on the Desktop — a week later there are 30 of them and you can't find anything. Use ~/projects/.
pitfalls.2: Deleting a folder with rm -rf without checking — it's gone forever. ls first, then rm.

0.question: Create your own ~/projects/ structure: at least 3 projects with meaningful names. One via Finder, two via mkdir.
0.hint: Names should answer "what is this?" 6 months later. "test" — bad. "monthly-reports-2026" — good.

1.question: Delete a temp folder both ways: once via the Trash (drag-to-trash), once via rm -r. Notice the difference.
1.hint: Trash → recoverable. rm -r → no, gone forever. When in doubt — Trash.

fw-1.title: Decide on a name and structure (naming rules)
fw-1.why: A folder name is a future `cd <this name>` command. Long / spaces / non-ASCII — you'll suffer every time.

instructions.0: Rule 1: ASCII only. No non-Latin letters.
instructions.1: Rule 2: instead of spaces — hyphens (or underscores). work-reports, not work reports.
instructions.2: Rule 3: the name answers "what's inside?" (≤ 30 chars). monthly-audits is better than stuff.
instructions.3: Rule 4: one folder — one topic. Don't dump different things into one.

fw-1.example:
Good: monthly-audits, claude-notes, sandbox-2026, website-redesign
Bad: "My projects", stuff, test, untitled folder, new folder (1)
fw-1.validate: You can explain to yourself: "This folder is about X, the name is short and clear."
fw-1.tip: If you plan to make a git repo from the folder — pick the name now. Renaming later is possible but noisy.

fw-2.title: Example 1 — Work audits (via the terminal)
fw-2.why: Scenario: you plan to do regular audits once a month. You need a shared folder for them.

instructions.0: Open the terminal.
instructions.1: Type: `mkdir -p ~/projects/monthly-audits/2026-may`. This creates both monthly-audits and the May subfolder.
instructions.2: Enter it: `cd ~/projects/monthly-audits/2026-may`.
instructions.3: Verify: `pwd` — ends with /monthly-audits/2026-may. Structure is ready to use.

fw-2.validate: You see the full path to 2026-may. Folder created, you're in it.
fw-2.tip: Subfolders by date (2026-may) follow the "new month = new folder" pattern. Scales very robustly.

fw-3.title: Example 2 — Notes and learning (via Finder/Explorer)
fw-3.why: Scenario: you're learning something new and want to keep notes. Visual is more convenient — that's fine.

instructions.0: macOS: open Finder → Cmd+Shift+H (return to home) → find the projects folder (or create it with Cmd+Shift+N).
instructions.1: Inside projects: right click → New Folder → type `learning-notes` → Enter.
instructions.2: Inside learning-notes — create two more: `claude` and `terminal-basics`.
instructions.3: Windows: open Explorer → navigate to C:\Users\<name>\projects → right click → New Folder. Repeat for subfolders.

fw-3.example:
The Finder structure:
projects/
  learning-notes/
    claude/
    terminal-basics/
fw-3.validate: In Finder/Explorer you see the tree: projects → learning-notes → claude / terminal-basics.
fw-3.tip: Terminal and Finder work on the same filesystem. A folder created in one is visible in the other. You can mix them.

fw-4.title: Example 3 — Temporary experiment (any method)
fw-4.why: Scenario: you want to experiment with something — you need a single-use folder you won't regret deleting.

instructions.0: Create it however you like: `mkdir -p ~/projects/sandbox` (terminal) OR via Finder.
instructions.1: Create some folders and files inside — anything. For example: `cd ~/projects/sandbox && touch test.txt && mkdir notes`.
instructions.2: Check the contents: `ls` — should show test.txt and notes.
instructions.3: Remember: this folder is a deletion candidate in step 5.

fw-4.prompt:
mkdir -p ~/projects/sandbox
cd ~/projects/sandbox
touch test.txt
mkdir notes
ls
fw-4.validate: In sandbox you see test.txt and notes/. Folder filled and ready for deletion.
fw-4.tip: touch creates an empty file in a second. Handy for quick tests. Windows equivalent: `New-Item test.txt` or `echo. > test.txt`.

fw-5.title: Clean deletion — two ways
fw-5.why: Learning to delete is as important as learning to create. Otherwise folders pile up endlessly.

instructions.0: Way 1 (safe) — via Finder/Explorer: open ~/projects/, drag sandbox to the Trash. Can be undone if you change your mind.
instructions.1: Way 2 (fast, irreversible) — `rm -rf ~/projects/sandbox` (mac/linux) or `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force ~/projects/sandbox` (PowerShell).
instructions.2: IMPORTANT: rm -rf deletes INSTANTLY, no Trash. Double-check the path before Enter.
instructions.3: Verify it's gone: `ls ~/projects/` — sandbox is no longer in the list.

fw-5.example:
Before: $ ls ~/projects/
monthly-audits  learning-notes  sandbox  my-first-project

After:
monthly-audits  learning-notes  my-first-project
fw-5.validate: ~/projects/ no longer contains sandbox. Experiment closed, working folders intact.
fw-5.tip: Never type rm -rf / or rm -rf ~/ — it deletes EVERYTHING. Always specify a concrete path and read it twice.

troubleshoot.rm: command not found on Windows: Use PowerShell with `Remove-Item -Recurse` or just Explorer + Delete.
troubleshoot.Trash doesn't restore on mac: Cmd+Shift+Delete empties the Trash. If you already emptied — files are lost (only Time Machine can recover, if enabled).

folders-workshop.trigger: You need a tidy folder structure for a Claude project — but no idea where to start.
outputs: 3 real folder structures created
Both GUI and command approaches mastered
A template for your future projects
folders-workshop.savings: ~30 min per new project + order in your files

welcome.title: Getting to know Claude
welcome.subtitle: What Claude is, what modes it has, and how to set it up for yourself
welcome.whatItIs: The very first lesson. Explains what Claude is, how it differs from other assistants, what its working modes are (Chat, Cowork, Code), and how to make it useful for your own tasks.
welcome.approach: Every step has buttons that open the right place for you. You do not need to hunt for things in the menus. Read, click, try.

outcomes.0: You know what Claude is and who built it
outcomes.1: You understand how Haiku, Sonnet and Opus models differ
outcomes.2: You can tell Chat, Cowork and Code apart
outcomes.3: You picked the version you need: the website, the app, or Code
outcomes.4: You know how to tune Claude with Custom Instructions and Projects

0.title: Light tasks
0.description: A letter, a translation, an explanation, a short summary. Chat at claude.ai is enough.

1.title: Long work on one task
1.description: Going through documents, multi-step tasks. Cowork in the desktop app fits.

2.title: Code and files
2.description: Programming, automation. Claude Code in the terminal is what you want.

pitfalls.0: Sticking to one mode only. Each one has its strengths. Different tools for different jobs.
pitfalls.1: Not setting Claude up for yourself. Without Custom Instructions it answers generically, with no idea about your context.
pitfalls.2: Ignoring model trade-offs. Haiku is fast but less accurate. Opus is smart but slow and pricey.

0.question: Open claude.ai and ask Claude to list three points that make it different from ChatGPT.
0.hint: Compare the answer with what you read in this lesson. It shows you how Claude thinks about itself.

w-1.title: What Claude is
w-1.why: To know who you are about to use.

instructions.0: Claude is a family of smart assistants that reply to you in text. They are built by a company called Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers.
instructions.1: Inside Claude there are three models of different power. Haiku is the fast and cheap one. Sonnet is the middle ground and the default. Opus is the smartest, for hard tasks.
instructions.2: You usually do not pick the model by hand. Claude picks the right one for the task. You can switch in settings when you need to.
instructions.3: Claude looks similar to ChatGPT in spirit, but differs in details. It has longer memory inside one chat, is more careful with facts, and stays calmer on touchy topics.

w-1.validate: You understand that Claude is built by Anthropic and comes in three models (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus).
w-1.tip: Sonnet covers about 95 percent of tasks. Switch to Opus only when you need deeper reasoning.

w-2.title: Three ways to work with Claude
w-2.why: Understand the difference between modes so you can pick yours.

instructions.0: Chat. A regular conversation in your browser or app. Ask a question, get an answer. Best for short tasks: letters, translations, explanations, idea brainstorming.
instructions.1: Cowork. A mode in the desktop app where Claude can work with your files, documents and even your screen, step by step. Best for long tasks: working through documents, writing long texts, doing analysis.
instructions.2: Code. A separate tool for programmers. It runs in the terminal on your computer. It can read and change code files, run commands. You only need it if you write code.
instructions.3: Next, we will walk through each of these three modes one by one. If you are not a programmer, the Code step is safe to skip.

w-2.validate: You remember the three names and what they are for: Chat for short tasks, Cowork for long ones, Code for programmers.
w-2.tip: Most people only need Chat. Cowork and Code are for those who want to go deeper.

w-3.title: Chat. The easiest way to start
w-3.why: This is the basic mode everyone starts with. Nothing to install.

instructions.0: Press the button below to open claude.ai in a new tab.
instructions.1: Sign in by email or through Google. Sign-up is free. You do not need a paid plan to begin.
instructions.2: After signing in you will see an input field. That is Chat.
instructions.3: Copy the question below and paste it into the field. Press send and read the answer.

w-3.prompt: In three simple sentences, tell me how you are different from ChatGPT and what you do best.
w-3.validate: You got a reply from Claude in Chat on [[node:pl-web-setup|claude.ai]].
w-3.tip: If the answer is too long, write: shorter, one sentence. Claude will get it.

w-4.title: Cowork. When the task is bigger than one question
w-4.why: For cases when you work on one topic for a while: writing a long text, going through a document, preparing a report.

instructions.0: Cowork lives in a separate app for Mac or Windows. Download it from Claude's website with the button below.
instructions.1: In Cowork you can give Claude files (documents, spreadsheets, images) or grant it screen access. It then works with them on its own, step by step.
instructions.2: Example tasks: go through these 50 pages and surface the key risks; read my email and draft replies; help me write a long article from this outline.
instructions.3: It is not for every task. If you only have a quick question, stay in Chat. Cowork pays off when there is ongoing work with your own files.

w-4.validate: You understand that Cowork is the desktop app for long tasks involving files.
w-4.tip: Serious Cowork work needs a Pro subscription. You can try it for free in a limited way.

w-5.title: Code. For people who work with code
w-5.why: If you write code or live in the terminal, this is Claude's most powerful mode. If you do not, feel free to skip.

instructions.0: Claude Code is a tool that runs in your terminal (the dark window with a command line on your computer).
instructions.1: It can read and edit code files directly on your disk, run commands, find bugs, refactor, explain unfamiliar code.
instructions.2: Install is one terminal command. It needs Node.js, a free program that runs commands. There is a dedicated tutorial that walks through it.
instructions.3: Code does not replace Chat or Cowork. It is a tool for developers, in addition to the rest.

w-5.validate: You understand: Code is a terminal tool, for people who work with code.
w-5.tip: If you are not a programmer, you can skip Code entirely and use only Chat. That is fine.

0.label: Install Claude Code step by step

w-6.title: Tuning. Make Claude yours with Custom Instructions
w-6.why: By default Claude answers in a generic way. To make it understand your context, you give it [[node:instructions|Custom Instructions]]. A short note about you.

instructions.0: Custom Instructions is a short message Claude sees inside every conversation of yours. You write your role, your industry, the tone you want, and what NOT to do.
instructions.1: Where to find it on the website: in claude.ai open your profile (top right), then Settings → Custom Instructions. The desktop app has a similar setting.
instructions.2: Example note: I am an accountant in a small business. Answer briefly, without fluff, in simple words. Do not give legal advice.
instructions.3: This changes the quality of answers a lot. Set it once and it always works. Update it when something starts to annoy you in the replies.

w-6.validate: You understand that Custom Instructions is your profile card for Claude.
w-6.tip: Do not write a wall of text. Five to ten lines about you and how you want to talk is more than enough.

w-7.title: Tuning. Projects for a series of related tasks
w-7.why: When you have a series of similar tasks, a Project is handy. It is a workspace with shared context.

instructions.0: A Project is a folder where you keep several chats on one topic. All chats inside a Project share knowledge and instructions.
instructions.1: Example: a Project called Marketing for company X. Inside, 20 chats with different questions about marketing. All of them share the same uploaded files: the brand guide, past reports, the yearly plan.
instructions.2: Where: on claude.ai look in the left menu for Projects, then New Project. Serious use needs a Pro plan.
instructions.3: If you keep working on one topic for weeks, a Project will save you hours of repeating context.

w-7.validate: You understand that a Project is a workspace for a series of related tasks.
w-7.tip: Do not make a Project for a single task. Use it for things that repeat.

w-8.title: What to do right now
w-8.why: Knowledge fades without action. Make at least one move.

instructions.0: If you are just meeting Claude for the first time, open claude.ai and ask your first question in Chat.
instructions.1: If you already like Claude and want to use it regularly, set up Custom Instructions. The quality jump is large.
instructions.2: If you need long work with files and documents, download the Claude app with Cowork support.
instructions.3: If you are a programmer and want the advanced mode, take the tutorial that installs Claude Code.

w-8.validate: You picked what to try next and made at least one click in that direction.
w-8.tip: Do not try to master everything in a day. Come back to the map when questions show up in your real work.

outputs: Clear sense of modes: Chat / Cowork / Code
Realistic expectations from Claude
Pick the first entry point
welcome.savings: ~a day of wandering vs 10 minutes of map

claude-cowork.title: Your first task with Claude Cowork
claude-cowork.subtitle: From open to result — autonomous workflow
claude-cowork.whatItIs: A hands-on walkthrough of Claude Cowork: open the Desktop app, connect a folder, describe a task as an outcome, let Claude run it, and review the results. You will complete a real file task from start to finish.
claude-cowork.approach: Describe WHAT you want, not HOW to do it. Claude figures out the steps. Start with a small, low-risk task on a test folder — not your critical files. Keep the Desktop app open the entire time.

outcomes.0: Opened Cowork and understand the interface
outcomes.1: Connected a specific folder (not your whole drive)
outcomes.2: Submitted an outcome-based task description
outcomes.3: Reviewed Claude's plan before approving it
outcomes.4: Checked the finished output and know how to iterate

0.title: File organization
0.description: Sort downloads, rename files by date, group by project — set it up once, run it weekly.

1.title: Document processing
1.description: Extract data from PDFs, summarize meeting notes, convert formats across a folder of files.

2.title: Scheduled automation
2.description: After mastering a task manually, use /schedule to run it automatically on a cadence.

cw-1.title: Open Cowork in Claude Desktop
cw-1.why: Cowork only exists in the Desktop app (Mac/Windows). The web version does not have it. You need a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan.

instructions.0: Download and install Claude Desktop from claude.ai/download if you haven't already.
instructions.1: Sign in with your Claude account (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise required).
instructions.2: In the Claude Desktop window, look for the 'Cowork' tab or button — it is separate from the regular chat.
instructions.3: Click it to open the Cowork interface. You will see a task input area and a section for connected folders.

cw-1.validate: You see the Cowork task interface — different from the regular chat.
cw-1.tip: Keep the Desktop app open during the entire tutorial. Cowork tasks stop the moment you close the app.

cw-2.title: Connect a folder
cw-2.why: Claude needs explicit permission to read and write files. You choose exactly which folder to expose — Claude cannot access anything outside it.

instructions.0: In the Cowork interface, find the 'Connect folder' or 'Add folder' option.
instructions.1: Choose a specific working folder — for example, a 'Cowork-test' folder on your Desktop.
instructions.2: Do NOT connect your entire Documents or Desktop root — start small and specific.
instructions.3: Confirm the connection. The folder should now appear as available in the Cowork context.

cw-2.validate: Your chosen folder appears as connected. Claude now has read/write access to it.
cw-2.tip: For your first task, create a test folder with a few non-critical files. This lets you experiment safely.

troubleshoot.Cannot find 'Connect folder' button: Check that you are in the Cowork tab, not the regular chat. The interface is different.
troubleshoot.Permission denied by OS: On macOS, go to System Settings → Privacy & Security → Files & Folders and grant Claude Desktop access.

cw-3.title: Describe your task as an outcome
cw-3.why: The key difference from regular chat: describe WHAT you want as a finished result, not the steps to get there. Claude plans the steps itself.

instructions.0: In the Cowork task field, type your task as an outcome.
instructions.1: Be specific: mention the folder, the type of files, and the desired end state.
instructions.2: Include the output format if it matters (e.g. 'create a summary as a .txt file').
instructions.3: Submit the task. Claude will show you a plan BEFORE starting.

cw-3.example:
Good: 'In the Cowork-test folder, group all files by extension into subfolders (e.g. /images, /docs, /other), then create a file called index.txt that lists what was moved and where.'

Bad: 'First check the folder, then create subfolders, then move each file...' — don't prescribe steps.
cw-3.validate: Claude presents a plan showing what it will do. Read it before approving.
cw-3.tip: If the plan looks wrong, type a correction before approving. It is faster to fix the plan than fix the output.

cw-4.title: Approve and monitor
cw-4.why: Cowork runs autonomously once approved. You can watch its progress or step away — both are valid. The key is keeping the Desktop app open.

instructions.0: Review Claude's plan carefully — check that it describes what you actually want.
instructions.1: Click Approve (or equivalent) to start the task.
instructions.2: Watch the progress indicator. Claude shows what it is doing at each step.
instructions.3: You can step away — Claude will continue. Come back when it signals completion.
instructions.4: Do not close the Desktop app. If you need to lock your screen, that is fine — just do not quit the application.

cw-4.validate: Task reaches 100% and Claude shows a summary of what was done.

troubleshoot.Task stopped unexpectedly: Most likely the Desktop app was closed or lost internet. Reopen it and check if the task can be resumed.
troubleshoot.Claude asks for permission mid-task: Some actions (like deletion) require your explicit approval. Read the request and approve or deny.

cw-5.title: Review the output and iterate
cw-5.why: Diligence: the first result is a strong draft, not necessarily final. Open the folder, check the files, and correct anything that missed the mark — in natural language.

instructions.0: Open the connected folder in your file manager and check the output.
instructions.1: Compare what Claude did against your original description.
instructions.2: If something is wrong, describe the issue in plain language in the Cowork task field.
instructions.3: For recurring tasks you are satisfied with, type /schedule to set up automatic runs.

cw-5.validate: Output matches your intent. You know how to describe corrections.
cw-5.tip: Say what is wrong ('the images folder is missing PDF files that have images embedded'), not how to fix it. Claude will figure out the correction.

ai-limitations.title: Claude's capabilities and limits
ai-limitations.subtitle: What Claude knows, what it doesn't, and how to work with both
ai-limitations.whatItIs: A practical guide to Claude's real boundaries. You will learn why Claude sometimes says wrong things confidently, what it literally cannot do, how the [[node:b-context|context window]] affects long sessions, and — most importantly — five strategies that turn limitations into non-issues.
ai-limitations.approach: Do not skip this tutorial thinking limitations are someone else's problem. Every user eventually hits them. The goal is not to avoid Claude but to use it in ways that make its limits irrelevant.

outcomes.0: Understand what a knowledge cutoff means and when it matters
outcomes.1: Recognize hallucinations before they cause problems
outcomes.2: Know what Claude structurally cannot do (and what it can with tools)
outcomes.3: Understand why long chats degrade in quality
outcomes.4: Have 5 concrete strategies to work around limitations

0.title: Fact-sensitive work
0.description: Legal, medical, financial, scientific — always verify Claude's factual claims against primary sources.

1.title: Research and writing
1.description: Use Claude for structure, reasoning, and drafting. Use web search or original sources for current facts.

2.title: Long projects
2.description: Break multi-day work into separate sessions or use Projects to maintain consistent context.

pitfalls.0: Trusting Claude's confident tone as evidence of accuracy — confidence and correctness are independent.
pitfalls.1: Asking about events after the training cutoff without enabling web search.
pitfalls.2: Running a 50-message conversation and wondering why quality drops — the context window is finite.

0.question: Ask Claude: 'What happened in the news this week?' Then ask: 'What is your training knowledge cutoff?' Compare the two answers. What does this tell you about when to use web search?
0.hint: Notice if Claude attempts an answer to the first question or declines. Either response tells you something about how to prompt it correctly.

1.question: Ask Claude a question on a niche topic you know well. Deliberately look for one plausible-sounding detail that might be wrong. Can you spot it?
1.hint: The goal is not to catch Claude — it is to practice the habit of Discernment from the 4D Framework.

al-1.title: The knowledge cutoff
al-1.why: Claude was trained on data up to a fixed date (~early 2026 for current models). It has no awareness of anything after that. This is not a bug — it is how language models work.

instructions.0: Understand: Claude's knowledge is a snapshot, not a live connection to the internet.
instructions.1: Claude Opus 4.7 has a training cutoff of approximately January 2026.
instructions.2: Asking about events after the cutoff: Claude will either refuse, say it doesn't know, or — in the worst case — hallucinate a plausible-sounding answer.
instructions.3: Solution: enable web search in claude.ai (the globe icon in the input bar) for any question involving recent events, current prices, live data, or recent news.

al-1.validate: You know when to turn on [[node:cap-search|web search]] and why.
al-1.tip: When in doubt about whether something is within Claude's cutoff, ask: 'Is this within your training data, or should I enable web search?' Claude will tell you honestly.

al-2.title: Hallucinations — what they are and why they happen
al-2.why: Claude can state incorrect facts with complete confidence. This is called a hallucination. It is the most dangerous limitation for users who do not know about it.

instructions.0: A hallucination happens when Claude 'fills a gap' in its knowledge with a plausible-sounding but false answer. The training process optimizes for helpfulness — and sometimes that means generating a confident answer instead of admitting uncertainty.
instructions.1: Hallucinations are more common on: niche topics, specific statistics and numbers, citations and paper references, recent events, and long chains of reasoning.
instructions.2: They are less common on: well-documented mainstream topics, general reasoning, coding, and math (though math errors do happen).
instructions.3: The key signal is NOT Claude's tone — a hallucinated answer sounds exactly as confident as a correct one.
instructions.4: Strategy: for any factual claim that matters, verify it in a primary source (official docs, papers, news).

al-2.validate: You understand that confident tone does not equal accurate content.
al-2.tip: Ask Claude to flag its uncertainty: add 'If you are not sure about any fact, say so explicitly' to your prompt. This helps — though it does not eliminate hallucinations entirely.

troubleshoot.How do I know if Claude is hallucinating: You often cannot tell from the response alone. The only reliable check is external verification. Treat Claude's factual claims as 'probably correct, needs spot-checking on anything that matters.'
troubleshoot.Claude said it is confident — does that: No. Confidence and accuracy are independent. Claude can be confident and wrong, or uncertain and right. Always verify facts that have real consequences.

al-3.title: The context window — why long chats degrade
al-3.why: Claude can only 'see' a fixed amount of text at once. When a conversation exceeds this limit, older messages fall out — Claude starts to lose track of earlier context, instructions, and decisions.

instructions.0: The context window is the total amount of text Claude can process at one time — your messages plus its responses.
instructions.1: As a conversation grows, earlier content gradually becomes invisible to Claude.
instructions.2: Signs of context degradation: Claude repeats things you already discussed, contradicts earlier decisions, asks for information you already provided, or gives shallower answers.
instructions.3: Solutions: use /compact in Claude Code to summarize context without losing history. In claude.ai, start a new chat for each distinct topic. Use Projects — they maintain persistent instructions even across separate chats.

al-3.validate: You know why multi-hour conversations in one chat produce worse results than shorter focused sessions.
al-3.tip: For long projects, use a Project with clear instructions rather than one endless chat. The [[node:p-instructions|Project instructions]] are always in context — your accumulated chat history is not.

al-4.title: What Claude structurally cannot do
al-4.why: Some limitations are architectural — no workaround exists, or a specific tool is required. Knowing these prevents frustration.

instructions.0: Cannot generate images — Claude produces text only. For images, use a dedicated image generation tool (DALL-E, Midjourney, etc.).
instructions.1: Cannot browse the internet by default — web search must be explicitly enabled.
instructions.2: Cannot take actions in other apps — unless Computer Use (Desktop, API) or an MCP integration is active.
instructions.3: Cannot remember across chats by default — use Memory (in settings) or Projects for persistence.
instructions.4: Cannot access real-time data (stock prices, weather, live scores) — enable web search or use an integration.
instructions.5: Cannot 'learn' from your correction permanently — corrections apply only to the current session unless saved to Custom Instructions or Memory.

al-4.validate: You know which limitations require a tool (web search, MCP, [[node:cap-computer|Computer Use]]) vs which are structural.
al-4.tip: Most 'cannot' items have a workaround via tools. Before assuming Claude can't do something, check if enabling web search, MCP, or Cowork would solve it.

al-5.title: Five strategies to work with limitations
al-5.why: Knowing limitations without strategies is just anxiety. These five approaches handle the vast majority of limitation-related problems.

instructions.0: 1. Enable web search for anything time-sensitive or fact-specific — the globe icon in claude.ai chat input.
instructions.1: 2. Ask Claude to flag uncertainty — add 'flag anything you are not confident about' to prompts that require factual accuracy.
instructions.2: 3. Verify what matters — treat Claude's output as a strong first draft, not a final source. Spot-check key facts.
instructions.3: 4. Use Projects instead of long chats — persistent instructions, fresh context each session, no context window degradation.
instructions.4: 5. Break large tasks — instead of one 3-hour session, run three 45-minute sessions with clear handoffs between them.

al-5.example:
Research task without strategies: one long chat, no web search, no verification → potential hallucinations, context degradation.

With strategies: Project with your research context, web search enabled, Claude flags uncertainty, you verify key statistics, each session has a clear scope → reliable, high-quality output.
al-5.validate: You have a mental checklist: web search on/off? Uncertainty flagging in prompt? Verification plan? Project or long chat?
al-5.tip: The 4D Framework's Discernment step IS this checklist. Limitations are not Claude's problem to solve — they are yours to design around.

Task type: facts, numbers, code, judgment
Access to a source of truth for verification
outputs: Checklist of where Claude is reliable vs unreliable
5 mitigation strategies (grounding, verification, chunking)

api-basics.title: Claude API for developers
api-basics.subtitle: Make your first API call and understand the primitives that power every Claude integration
api-basics.whatItIs: A hands-on introduction to the Anthropic API. You will get an API key, make your first request, understand the core primitives (messages, roles, system prompts, tokens, streaming), and learn the patterns you will use in every Claude-powered application you build.
api-basics.approach: Every concept is shown with a working code example. Read the explanation, run the code, see the result. By the end you will have the mental model to build anything from a simple script to a production-grade AI feature.

outcomes.0: Obtain an API key and make your first working API call
outcomes.1: Understand the messages array, roles (user/assistant/system), and why the structure matters
outcomes.2: Know how tokens work and how to estimate and control cost
outcomes.3: Stream responses so users see output immediately
outcomes.4: Use the official Python and TypeScript SDKs
outcomes.5: Know the five most common integration mistakes and how to avoid them

2.title: AI agents and pipelines
2.description: The Messages API is the foundation of every Claude agent. Tool use, multi-turn memory, and orchestration all build on these same primitives.

pitfalls.0: Hardcoding the API key in source code — use environment variables or a secrets manager.
pitfalls.1: Setting max_tokens too high by default — you pay for output tokens whether you use them or not.
pitfalls.2: Not streaming long responses — users stare at a blank screen while waiting for a full response to generate.
pitfalls.3: Building multi-turn chat manually without tracking the messages array — context gets lost.
pitfalls.4: Ignoring rate limits — production apps need retry logic with exponential backoff.

0.hint: Use the anthropic Python SDK. The messages array should have one user message: f'Summarize {topic} in exactly 3 sentences.'
